This unit is equipped for electronic warfare, specialized in detecting or jamming enemy electronic devices, radar or signals.
AIRLIFT units can be transported by helicopters featuring the AIRLIFTER trait.
This vehicle is designed to tow heavy equipment, such as artillery, on the battlefield.  Prime movers range from jeeps and heavy trucks to dedicated artillery tractors.
This unit is equipped with radio direction-finding systems. Enemy radio signals are intercepted and used to triangulate the approximate position of the enemy unit.

Anti-Aircraft (AA) guns are designed to take out low-flying airborne targets. They are frequently emplaced in dual or even quadruple quick-traversing mounts with high rates of fire and elevation. Older models might lack guidance systems, limiting their use, while more advanced systems feature rangefinders, targeting computers and radar.

A rotary cannon is a multi-barrelled weapon capable of firing a large quantity of projectiles extremely fast. Rotary cannons encompass a variety of calibers, firing systems and number of barrels, and can also be known as Gatling or miniguns.

This type of quick-firing weapon projects a destructive hail of fire onto a target. A rotary cannon is a common armament on helicopters and aircraft, useful against ground and aerial targets, or in an anti-tank role.
Although UAV doesn't have ECM, they are very hard to target effectively by enemy fire. Also, the operator being safe on the ground, an UAV doesn't suffer from stress nor evacuate automatically.
This unit represents an army's crème de la crème: highly trained professionals, well-equipped and with more combat veterancy than regular troops.

False Flag units are dedicated special military troops covertly dressed in civilian clothes or even enemy uniforms. Using this ruse during infiltration or special operations is a risky tactic, creating surprise and confusion, but might breach the laws of war.

An anti-tank guided missile (ATGM) is designed to destroy armored vehicles. ATGMs range from crew-served weapons operated by a small team to vehicle-mounded and even long-range advanced models on a helicopter or close air support aircraft. Older generation missiles need to be actively guided onto the target, while more modern variants home in automatically.

ATGMs are very effective weapons against any kind of vehicle, as long as the line of sight is maintained.
Leader units grant +1 Veterancy level to all nearby units. Classified as Command units, they can also capture Command Zones.
Sniper units gain an extra level of Stealth, plus a +500% damage boost and Accuracy bonus when not moving. The unit must remain still for at least 10 seconds for this effect to trigger.

An unguided or “dumb” bomb is an explosive employed by aircraft or helicopters against enemy ground units.
Simple and destructive, unguided bombs are also known as gravity bombs. A disadvantage is that bombs dropped as a payload need to have the user fly over a target, and a rather inaccurate. Unguided bombs can come in many shapes and sizes, from small bomblets to bunker busters targeting hardened targets.

Mortars are indirect-fire crew-served infantry weapons capable of lobbing shells in high trajectories across medium distances.
Mortars come in various calibers, from 50mm to 120mm to the occasional massive 240mm. Caliber size determines their range, how easily they can be transported, rate of fire, and destructive power. Some larger units are vehicle-mounted on dedicated carriers, allowing quick displacement after shooting. Capable of firing off different types of rounds, from high-explosive to smoke or illumination, mortars provide indispensable organic fire support on the battlefield.

Mortars come in various calibers, from 50mm to 120mm to the occasional massive 240mm. Caliber size determines their range, how easily they can be transported, rate of fire, and destructive power. Some larger units are vehicle-mounted on dedicated carriers, allowing quick displacement after shooting. Capable of firing off different types of rounds, from high-explosive to smoke or illumination, mortars provide indispensable organic fire support on the battlefield.

This unit is made up of former soldiers, National Guardsmen, or other types of reservists with previous military experience. Depending on age, they possess a degree of training and general familiarity with an army’s weapons, tactics, and equipment.
Prime movers are transport units capable of carrying towed units such as artillery or air defense systems. They might also be used to transport infantry, weapon teams and crew-served weapons.

A Gatling gun is a multi-barrelled automatic rotary cannon capable of shooting a massive quantity of rounds extremely fast.
Using an electronic firing mechanism, a modern Gatling gun (also known as minigun) can fire so quickly it is in danger of running out of ammunition within seconds. Gatling guns are often cumbersome weapons and are relegated to be used on aircraft or stable land platforms. They can be employed as a close-in defensive system to saturate a target area by throwing a hail of fire, an anti-aircraft gun, or even an airborne anti-tank weapon able to punch through the weak top plating of many armored vehicles.

A rocket is an unguided warhead-equipped projectile powered by a rocket engine. Amongst other things, it differs from missiles by the lack of active guidance systems.

Artillery units equipped with rockets compensate for a lack of accuracy with the ability to quickly saturate and destroy an area with a large number of rockets.

They can be employed as a close-in defensive system to saturate a target area by throwing a hail of fire, an anti-aircraft gun, or even an airborne anti-tank weapon able to punch through the weak top plating of many armored vehicles.

A grenade launcher can lob projectiles across short distances. These are crew-served weapons, sometimes mounted on vehicles. Certain models use semi- or even fully automatic fire mechanisms.

Grenade launchers can be both used in a direct fire or indirect fire role as a rapid mortar-like weapon. They are effective against enemy infantry.
Laser Designator units grant an Accuracy bonus to Guided Munitions while the target is kept within line of sight.

This unit is specifically trained and equipped for operations in mountains and other rugged terrain. Their logistical footprint is lighter, with mountain warfare units frequently employing specialized vehicles and weapons.

Howitzers are artillery guns capable of indirect fire across long distances. They take time to prepare and shoot. Towed or self-propelled units are available, as well as a variety of calibers, indicative of max range and shell power.

Anti-Aircraft units are designed to combat aircraft and helicopters. They use anti-aircraft guns, guided missiles, or a combination of both. Sensors, such as radar or infrared, provide target tracking and guidance. Air defense units, including MANPAD teams, are typically optimized for either short-, medium- or long range.

Guided Munitions can be bombs or shells, fired directly or indirectly, which receive an Accuracy bonus on laser-designated targets.

False Flag units are easily mistaken for neutral or even friendly troops in the heat of battle. In combat, the threat level for a False Flag unit is lower than any other unit. This means they will always be targeted last by enemy forces.
This unit is equipped with a Counter-Battery Radar, designed to detect incoming artillery projectiles. Tracking their trajectories, it can locate the enemy weapon system’s ground position.

A transport unit's primary mission is to swiftly carry infantry and other units across the battlefield. Transport vehicles come in a variety of sizes, from fast jeeps and trucks to armed APCs, IFVs or even helicopters. Some transports act as prime movers, towing artillery and air defense systems.
This transport vehicle is designed to move infantry units, including recon and weapon teams.
A long range semi active missile, operated from a very long distance.

A medium machine gun is capable of automatic fire at medium ranges. Belt-fed machine guns are light enough to be carried by an individual soldier, but most often needs a small crew to be operated effectively. Medium machine guns are commonly mounted on vehicles including as a coaxial weapon.

The medium machine gun is an effective weapon against infantry across short- to medium ranges.

Anti-Air (AA) guns are weapons designed to take out fast-moving airborne targets.
These types of guns are frequently emplaced in quick traversing turrets with a high rate of fire and elevation. In this way, with more advanced systems using targeting computers and radar, they can track and shoot at aircraft and helicopters at a moment’s notice. AA guns are often found in dual or even quadruple mounts. In addition, these guns are frequently used for great effect in a direct-fire role against lightly armored ground targets.

A flamethrower is a destructive weapon projecting a controllable jet of flames. Using liquid fuels or other incendiary mixtures such as napalm, flamethrowers can be vehicle-mounted or man-portable. 

Although they have a very short range, flamethrowers are highly effective against infantry, even behind cover.
Ground Surveillance Radar units receive a +1 Optics level when not moving.
This recon unit is equipped with a portable Ground Surveillance Radar, detecting targets beyond visual range. Once deployed, it needs to remain stationary to function.

Electronic Warfare aircraft have powerful Electronic Counter Measures (ECM) equipment which they project in an area of effect. Within this range, any enemy air defense radar is disrupted, with the target unit's weapons losing 20% Accuracy. The Electronic Warfare aircraft also has SEAD-level of Air Optics, allowing them to spot enemy units equipped with radar from afar.

Unguided air-to-ground rockets are fired from aircraft and helicopters at ground targets.
A common weapon, rockets normally lack an active guidance system, separating them from missiles. A simple and easy-to-use weapon - though not very accurate - rockets are convenient in a short-range or area saturation role. Carrying various types of warheads, rockets are frequently fired from rocket pods in devastating salvoes.

The standard weapon for a large number of frontline soldiers, the battle rifle is effective against enemy troops at intermediate ranges.
Heavy and powerful, battle rifles are very accurate and deadly when the shooter is immobile, but quite less than an assault rifle on the move, especially since it uses smaller magazines. Most assault rifles can be modified with accessories such as scopes, foregrips, night vision devices, or single-shot grenade launchers.

The 16e Pantserdivisie, or 16th Armored Division, was one of the two original formations of the Belgian Army’s I (BE) Corps, forward deployed in NORTHAG from 1951. While Belgium never wavered in its commitment to NATO, for most of the Cold War, its underfunded bilingual armed forces were regarded as one of the least powerful in the alliance. By the end of the 1980s, however, serious efforts were made to modernize and introduce new weaponry in the Belgian Armed Forces.

Close to a mechanized infantry formation, the 16e Pantserdivisie is reinforced with well-trained reconnaissance troops. It also includes Luxembourg's diminutive contribution to NATO: a light infantry battalion equipped with American-made materiel. One of the most recent Belgian acquisitions is the AIFV armored vehicle family, transporting Mech. Fusiliers infantry. Armor support takes the form of the Leopard 1 (BE), including the rare Leopard 1A5 (BE). The division’s recon forces are prolific users of the CRV(T) family of vehicles, from Spartan to Scimitar light tanks, backed by ESR special forces available as 6-man recon or 2-man sniper teams. A handful A.109HA helicopters have been pressed into active service, which, together with the Gepard 2B SPAAGs, Épervier UAVs, Mistral AA MANPADS, and the Belgian Air Force’s F-16A with HE and Cluster payloads, constitute some of the most advanced equipment of the Belgian Army.

The Division Mobilisation was the Belgian Army’s umbrella designation for various interior troops called upon to reinforce I (BE) Corps in West Germany in case of conflict. If an enemy breakthrough or airborne assaults threatened Belgian territory directly, this NATO rear-area formation would also provide local security for key sites and army assets. Division Mobilisation included a collection of Territorial regiments, regular light infantry, plus Gendarmerie military police and its armored squadron, plus shadowy stay-behind special forces. Older stockpiled equipment from weapon depots, as well as heavy anti-air units, would also fall under the division’s command.

The Division Mobilisation, while fielding older weaponry, is a mechanized battlegroup at heart. This includes the light M41 tank, the heavier M47 main battle tank, M75 APC and command vehicle, BDX wheeled APCs, plus FN 4RM 62F Gendarmerie armored vehicles. Chasseurs Ardennais light infantry will deploy side-by-side with False Flag-traited SDRA8 saboteur squads. Artillery ranges from the World War II-era Long Tom 155mm and M1 8-inch 203mm howitzers to slightly more modern M108A2 105mm and M55 203mm self-propelled units. Potent anti-air cover is provided by HSS.630-3 triple 20mm and Bofors M/54 57mm heavy AA guns, and I-Hawk SAM.

The 1st Canadian Division had a distinguished combat record spanning both World Wars, though it was mostly inactive during the Cold War. Reactivation came in 1988, when the formation was used to consolidate the Canadian land forces based in Lahr, southern West Germany. The overarching Canadian Forces Europe, including the 1st Canadian Air Division, was to be placed under French command of SOUTHAG in case of war.

The 1st Canadian Division counts on two infantry brigades, the heavy 4 Canadian Mechanized Brigade-Group, and the much lighter 5e Groupe-Brigade Mécanisé du Canada. Infantry follow their parent brigade in strength and mobility, from Mech. Rifles, Tank Hunters, CFMP military police, or Reserve squads with Canadian-designated small arms. They deploy in either tracked M113 or wheeled Grizzly APCs, including a rare Grizzly CP escort. Canada’s main battle tank in the late Cold War is the Leopard C1, a Leopard 1A3 upgraded with more accurate fire-control systems. Another interesting unit is the Cougar, acting as a fire support vehicle. The fast CL-89 drone provides valuable eyes in the sky, while the unique ADATS fires dual-ATGM and AA missiles. The Royal Canadian Air Force fields the state-of-the-art CF-18 (F-18) in a variety of different load-outs, backed by CF-5A, Silver Star MK.3AT trainers, and EF-101B Electric Voodoo EW planes.

The Czechoslovak People’s Army 19. Motostřelecká Divize, or 19th Motor Rifle Division, was created in 1958 in Plzeň, its home base for the duration of the Cold War. The ČSLA’s motorized rifle division, much like other Warsaw Pact allies, was structured along the Soviet Army lines. In the event of war, reorganizations would see the 19th Motorized lose one of its infantry regiments but, in turn, gain the famous 22nd Airborne Brigade and a helicopter regiment. 

The 19. Motostřelecká Divize features a strong core of logistical and command units, from the T813 heavy supply truck to the OT-62/R4MT command APC. They serve the capable but limited number of Motostřelci mechanized infantry, backed by a handful of elite airborne Výsadkáři special forces, including weapon teams equipped with recoilless rifles, Igla AA, and Konkurs ATGMs. Supporting arms, such as artillery with its domestically-made Dana self-propelled howitzers, the 120mm mortar-carrying Prám-S and the long-range SHK 2S7, can deploy side-by-side with T-72M1 tanks, advanced T-55AM1s, OT PTRK Konkurs tank destroyers, and PLRK Kub mobile SAMs. Several other potent units round out the divisional arsenal, including the dual-Jammer and SIGINT-traited Mi-17Z2 helicopter, MiG-29 air defense fighters, the Su-25 ground attack aircraft in large numbers, and the Mi-24V gunship in various configurations.

The 1. Tanková Divize, or 1st Tank Division, was formed in 1958 by the Československá ľudová armáda or Czechoslovak People’s Army (ČSLA). The ČSLA’s political allegiance to the socialist cause was seriously questioned after the Prague Spring of 1968, with low morale and strict Soviet oversight still felt by the late 1980s. However, thanks to Czechoslovakia’s well-established industrial base, its armed forces were considered one of the best-equipped in the Warsaw Pact, from small arms to IFVs and aircraft. 

The 1. Tanková Divize, as part of the ČSLA’s 1st Army, was to be used as a well-trained exploitation force. The division’s mechanized troops rely heavily on the capable T-72M, including the T-72S, and the BMP-2, both produced domestically under license. Regular Motostřelci infantry and Ženist combat engineers can also deploy in BVP-1 and OT-64 APCs (Polish-made SKOT). The division’s artillery forces are well-equipped, ranging from M Vz.52 82mm mortars, self-propelled SH M 2S4 Tulipan 240mm mortars, and an SVO demining vehicle with its massive, 240mm short-range mine-clearing rockets. Recon is another category that shines, with units such as SHPZ recon special forces, BPVZ Svatava radar-recon, and the Tu-143 recon drone. The Československé letectvo, or Czechoslovak Air Force, deploys either the MiG-23BN with a variety of ground strike payloads or MiG-23MLA in an air defense role.

The Czechoslovakian 2. Motostřelecká Divize, or 2nd Motorized Rifle Division, was part of the frontline 1st Army located on the southern frontier of the communist country. Guarding the tri-border area of Czechoslovakia, West Germany, and Austria, border guards form an integral part of this Warsaw Pact battlegroup. In case of war, the formation would have been one of the more capable units of the ČSLA, though it would rely heavily on territorial battalions to shore up any enemy breakthrough or flanking attempts. 

As a mechanized division, the 2. Motostřelecká Divize fields not only plentiful OT-64 APCs, but also lavishly equipped with modernized T-55AM2 tanks, including the ATGM-wielding AM2B variant, while also being in the process of upgrading its tank regiment to the capable T-72M1. Older T-54Bs round out the battlegroup’s armor force, which will fight side-by-side with regular Motostřelci and reservists, larger Pohraničníci border guards featuring the Mountaineer trait, and various infantry scouts.  Several potent units can be deployed from the division’s arsenal, such as the R-330T Taran MT-LB-based SIGINT vehicle, the light M-46 130mm howitzers and RM-70 Cluster-equipped multiple rocket launchers, sourced from army corps detachments. The older SU-7BKL “bomb truck” ground attack aircraft will be covered by more modern Su-22M4, MiG-21MA, and MiG-23MLA as air superiority fighters.

The Czechoslovakian 303. Tanková Divize, or 303rd Tank Division, was planned to be activated during war in a rear-area home defense role. The division’s cadre would come from training personnel, rounded out by reservists and territorial militia, with equipment drawn from secondary storage sites. A sprinkling of modern vehicles and weaponry would give the 303rd Tank Division a boost in combat power.

The battlegroup counts on numerous infantry, fielding weaponry of varying quality and age. They can deploy en masse, from Lidové milice to large Záložníci reservist squads in OT-65VP and OT-810/R2 half-tracks, amongst others. While an armored formation in name, the division’s large tank force mainly consists of older vehicles, including T-34/85M and SD-100 tank destroyers, backed by slightly less venerable T-54Bs, and a handful of T-72M-E2. Other vintage equipment includes KH Vz.18/47N 152mm howitzers, PTK Vz.52 85mm anti-tank guns, and the Mi-4 helicopter. One of the division’s strong points are its AA defenses, ranging from the massive PLRK Krug SAM to an array of towed AA guns, such as the large PLK KS-30 130mm. Air cover is potent, with a mix of lighter L-39 jet trainers pressed into close air support service to the ubiquitous MiG-21MF and the Su-22M4 in ground-strike roles.

The Royal Danish Army’s largest and one of the few standing formations during the Cold War was the Jyske Division, or Jutland Division. Raised in 1951 and headquartered in Frederica, the Hæren formation was part of Western Command and was to be transferred to NATO’s LANDJUT in case of war.
The small Danish army would rely on the Jyske Division to guard the Jutland peninsula from enemy invasion, including supporting its West German allies in Schleswig-Holstein.
Likely slow to mobilize, the Jyske Division in the late 1980s amounted to three mechanized brigades and one artillery brigade, plus several independent battalions.

The Jyske Division deploys the capable Panserinfanteri mechanized infantry, Ingeniører combat engineers, and motorized Infanteri Pnæv squads, supported by heavily armed Jægere special forces. Transports available include Bedford M2JP trucks, M113A1, and Laro jeeps.
Second-generation Leopard 1 DK main battle tanks, plus the upgraded Leopard 1A5-DK, provide armor support, further backed by older Centurion Mk.V with their original 20-pounder tank guns, and modernized M41-DK1 recon tanks.
Other noteworthy units are the M113A2 PNMK, a Danish-modified APC with the Oerlikon 25mm autocannon, the PVH Fennec helicopter, and the Home Guard’s SEP/VLK long-range recon squads.
The Royal Danish Air Force protects the skies with both the F-16A in a variety of load-outs, and the iconic Swedish-made Saab 35 Draken.

The Østre Landsdelskommand, or Eastern Command, encompassed all units earmarked for the defense of the Danish Isles, specifically Zealand (home to Copenhagen) and the remote Bornholms garrison.
The independent Zealand Brigades and Zealand Battlegroups formed the nucleus of the formation’s fighting power, supplemented by a large contingent of Danish Hjemmeværnet, or Home Guard. Comparable to other reserve arms, this latter land-branch of the Danish Armed Forces was highly motivated and trained, stood up to oppose any kind of enemy invasion during the Cold War.‌

The Østre Landsdelskommand is a reserve formation which can deploy plentiful infantry, from regular Infanteri to more numerous 12-man Home Guard squads and Danish Navy’s frogmen, the Frømænd.
Armored vehicles are notably old and include Centurion Mk. V/2 DK, M41-DK1 light tanks, and even HJV M/10, which are re-used World War II-era M10c Achilles tank destroyers.Air defenses are formidable, from the LRKT Hamlet MANPAD teams to I-Hawk and Bedford Firling 12,7mm gun trucks. The Danish Navy deploys the S-61A helicopter, either as a radar recon or supply unit.
The Flyvevåbnet, or Royal Danish Air Force, provides potent air cover with its fleet of Saab F-35 Draken, in air superiority and close air support roles. The U.S. Marine Corps also comes to the aid of its NATO allies with its F/A-18A in fighter and SEAD loadouts.

The French 11e Division Parachutiste was created in 1971 by regrouping various fast-reaction and paratrooper forces. While French divisions were generally smaller than comparable NATO formations, this Cold War battlegroup was the exception, featuring no less than seven airborne infantry regiments. It formed half of France’s quick Force Terrestre d’Intervention, deploying to Chad, Zaïre, and Lebanon. In the event of war, the 11e Division Parachutiste would rapidly deploy to the most pressing NATO sectors in West Germany.

The 11e Division Parachutiste counts on strong, fast-moving infantry, with plenty of units featuring the Airborne trait. These include veteran Chasseurs-Paras and Sapeurs-Paras, elite Legionnaires-Paras, plus supporting weapon teams and vehicles. A second wave is composed of Aeromobiles in Puma helicopters and Reservistes infantry. French materiel clearly focuses on mobility, with examples such as the VBL armored car, the light ERC-90 Sagaie wheeled tank, the recon AML-90, and the VLRA Milan. The Gazelle Celtic in anti-air configuration, Puma medium helicopters in supply and command roles, and the Puma Pirate as a gunship make up the division’s helicopter force. The Armée de l’Air provides formidable air cover, from ground-attack planes such as the Mirage 5F and Jaguar in a variety of configurations to SEAD and cluster bombers. Fighters include Mirage 2000C RDI and Mirage F1C-200, plus the advanced F1 CT variant with laser-guided bombs.

The French 152e Division d’Infanterie was a reserve formation based near Plateau d’Albion in southeastern France. Its Cold War mission was simple: to protect the critically important French nuclear arsenal and missile silos at Base Aérienne 200 from any prospective enemy incursion, sabotage, or air assault. Formed in 1979 as a training unit with a cadre of professional soldiers as part of the 5e Division Militaire, additional reservist units would be attached in case of conflict. This includes two Régiment d’Infanterie de Marine, or naval infantry regiments, rounded out by regular infantry, armored cavalry, and combat engineers.

The 152e Division d’Infanterie counts on Base Aérienne 200’s own defenses to boost its firepower, including heavy Commandos de l’Air security special forces, a smattering of Reserviste squads, backed by Marsouins naval infantry and the VIB APC available in a range of configurations. The AML-90 armored cars can be deployed en masse, while anti-air forces are likewise potent, from the Cerbere twin 20mm guns to the formidable Crotale SAM. Air cover is very capable, from nimble Alpha Jet Es to older Fouga Magister, with additional French Aéronavale Naval Aviation F-8P Crusader and Super Etendard fighter-bombers providing key close air support.

The French 5e Division Blindée fought with distinction in World War II. Afterward, the armored division remained stationed in West Germany. While France officially withdrew from NATO’s integrated command in the 1960s, its forces remained closely aligned with the military alliance. The 5e Division Blindée was a mobile tank division, with French doctrine emphasizing speed over armor. At the first sign of war, the division as part of a French vanguard, would rapidly deploy to reinforce SOUTHAG-based West Germans and Americans.

The 5e Division Blindée includes the AMX-30B2, the French main battle tank of the era, and, while lightly armored, it is fast with a powerful tank gun. One of the latest variants was the AMX-30B2 Brenus with ERA reactive armor. Mechanized infantry are available as 8-man Chasseurs squads in AMX-10P IFVs or 10-man Grenadier-Voltigeurs in VAB APCs, backed by Commandos special forces. ATGM carriers firing long-range HOT 2 missiles can be deployed as the VAB Mephisto and AMX-10 HOT. The 5e Division Blindée fields strong supporting arms, from quick recon AMX-10RC Surblindé to the advanced AMX AuF1 155mm self-propelled artillery, anti-air TRM-2000 Tarasque gun trucks, and radar-controlled AMX-13 DCA. Air assets include Mirage 5 F and Jaguar ground attack planes, while Mirage III E fighters and more modern Mirage F1C-200 contest the skies for air superiority.

The French 6e Division Légère Blindée, or 6th Light Armoured Division, traced its origins to a World War I cavalry division, also seeing action in World War II. During the Cold War, the formation was reorganized several times, before becoming famous as the late-1980s armored first of the Forces d'Action Rapide, France's counter-operational maneuver corps. Due to its very light organization and arsenal, and great emphasis on battlefield mobility, the division’s ability to deploy on very short notice was unrivaled in the French Army.

The 6e Division Légère Blindée is an extremely fast battlegroup, forgoing tracked vehicles or other cumbersome units for additional speed. It can also count on a large number of Légion Etrangère infantry, the Foreign Legion, deployable with extra veterancy in regular, command, Sapeurs, ATGM, and weapon teams. They are further represented with several unique vehicles from Legion. Mo-120-RT61 120mm mortar, VAB PM-81 Legion self-propelled mortar, AMX-10RC SB Legion, and P4 Milan jeeps, amongst others. The predominance of mobility leads to an eclectic mix of units, such as the Gazelle CP command helicopter and the Berliet GBU 15 supply truck, with a particularly cutting-edge weapon being the TRF-1 155mm towed artillery gun. Recon is likewise a divisional strong suit, from Spahis recon squads to AMX-10RC Legion recon armored vehicles to the SA.330B Puma Orchidee recon helicopter.

The French Division du Rhin was one of the shortest-lived formations to exist at the end of the Cold War. This division consolidated several rear-area and second-echelon troops in the French First Army, including reinforcements from the 7e Division Blindée and West German territorial troops. As part of SOUTHAG, it had one key mission: to protect the transfer of multiple divisions from France to southern West Germany in case of war, defending and organizing traffic around the critical Rhine bridges.

The Division du Rhin is made up of plentiful combat engineers and their equipment, as well as supporting infantry, including Reservistes, plus a powerful umbrella of anti-air units. They are backed by Sapeurs, weapon teams, Gendarmes Mobiles - transportable in police-blue Traffic Gendarmerie or VBRG armored cars - and West German Jäger squads. Vehicles and weaponry are noticeably of older origins, from M47 Dozer and AMX-13 tanks, the AMX-13 T75 featuring the venerable SS.11 missile, to F3 Automoteur 155mm self-propelled artillery and M55 Maxson quad AA. A sprinkling of advanced units can deploy, including LRM multiple rocket launchers and several aircraft, such as Alpha Jet Es, Mirage III Es with anti-tank and SEAD payloads, Mirage 2000C RDM in air defense roles, and Mirage 5 F fighter-bombers.

The Royal Netherlands Army’s 4e Divisie was part of the I (NL) Corps, guarding the northernmost sector of NORTHAG, including the exposed Covering Force Area near the Inner German Border. Due to political considerations, Dutch war plans saw the bulk of the Corps’ units based in the Netherlands. An optimistically planned mobilization during conflict would likely not have been as rapid as envisioned, with Dutch forces in West Germany having to fend for themselves for much longer than anticipated.

The 4e Divisie’s mainstay is the state-of-the-art Leopard 2A4, giving the mechanized infantry division a serious boost in armored firepower. Older Leopard 2A1 and Leopard 1NL variants are also available. The same AIFV series of APCs and IVFs as found in the Belgian Army, designated the YPR-765 in Landmacht service, can deploy, from the convolutedly-named PRRDR radar recon, to command, supply, cargo, and a TOW-2 equipped YPR-765-PRAT. Mechanized infantry comes as Pantserinfanterie and Genie combat engineers, with Natres reservists filling out the ranks. Recon is potent and includes Verkenners recon and Korps Commandotroepen special forces squads, the 25mm autocannon-fielding M113 C&V, and the Cheetah PRLT, which is a Dutch variant of the Gepard SPAAG. The Royal Netherlands Air Force was one of the first NATO partners to field the F-16, which is backed in the sky by the older NF-5A Freedom Fighter in a variety of roles.

The Dutch Commando LegerKorpsAchtergebied, or simply CKLA, stood for Rear Area Command, a war-activated command to be created as part of the I (NL) Corps fighting in NORTHAG. It would have been used to secure the immediate rear of the main Dutch divisions close to the Inner German Border. The main component of this Landmacht formation was the 101. Infanteriebrigade, supported by the VerkBat 105 recon battalion. The infantry, mostly recently called up mobilized reservists with near-regular training and equipment levels, would safeguard strategic rear-area assets, from long-range anti-air units to heavy artillery guns.

The CKLA’s arsenal features a host of capable units, from DAF YHZ-2300 Vracht heavy supply trucks, Beveiling security troops, military police’s M113 C&V KMAR APCs, to the iconic YP-408 wheeled armored vehicle series available in a variety of configurations, including YP-408 PWCO command, YP-408 PWRDR radar recon, and YP-408 PWAT tank destroyer. Older-generation Leopard 1V main battle tanks fight side-by-side with a handful of the heavy-hitting Leopard 2A4(B). Supporting arms range from cluster-equipped M270 MLRS, modernized M114/39 155m towed guns, or self-propelled M110A2 heavy artillery. Much like its ground forces, air cover is varied, from Dutch F-16A in air defense roles, American F-16C used for close air support, NF-F5A fighter-bombers, plus F-4E and F-4G Phantoms in both air superiority and SEAD roles.

The Polish People’s Army’s 15 Dywizja Zmechanizowana, or 15th Mechanized Infantry Division, was earmarked for any planned offensive on the Danish Isles. Acting as a follow-up second-echelon wave to the first assault corps, the formation would be ferried to hostile shores in order to mop up any remaining opposition. Most of the division’s manpower was made up of reservist forces, with a sprinkling of regular soldiers.
The 24th Mortar Brigade would beef up the formation’s organic artillery with older, but still potent systems. Additional support in any wartime invasion across the Baltic Sea would come from East Germany’s naval infantry and Soviet air power.

The 15 Dywizja Zmechanizowana counts on numerous Rezerwiści squads, deployable in Topas-2A or LO-1800 transports, as well as reserve Rez. Zwiadowcy scout teams. Nationale Volksarmee’s “armored sailors,” the Panzermatrosen, can also deploy with SPW-70 APCs, landing on hostile shores alongside Polish Formoza special forces squads.
Artillery is plentiful, from M43 160mm to super-heavy M240 240mm mortars, plus A-19 122mm towed guns, and BM-14M and BM-24M multiple rocket launchers. Older-generation tanks include the upgraded T-55U and the slightly more venerable T-55A and T-55AS with mine-clearing rockets.
Three different Warsaw Pact air forces fly top cover, from Polish Su-7BKL with Napalm and unarmed Electronic Warfare variants, East German MiG-21bis in air defense roles, and highly capable Soviet Su-27S air superiority fighters.

The 20 "Warszawska" Dywizja Pancerna, or 20th “Warsaw” Tank Division, was created in 1951 in Szczecinek, being turned into a full-fledged armored formation in 1955. The division took on the traditions of the 1st Warsaw Cavalry Brigade in 1967 and, as such, received the distinguishing name "Warszawska.” It was the sole armored division of the northernmost Polish 1st Army, directed to attack either Denmark or Hamburg in conjunction with the East German 5th Army.

The 20 "Warszawska" Dywizja Pancerna featured one of the few BWP-2 (Polish service name for the BMP-2) battalions in the Polish People’s Army, with the IFV bringing to battle the Piechota mechanized infantry squads. The armored spearhead of the division is formed by T-55 and T-72 tanks, including the domestically upgraded T-72M2 Wilk, further supported by the very capable, wheeled AHS WZ.77 Dana 152mm self-propelled artillery. A ground radar-equipped special forces Rozp. Specjalne (GSR) team can deploy in either Polish-made Honker jeeps or BRDM-1 armored cars. Rotorcraft are few and far between, but do include the diminutive Mi-2 in Mi-2US recon and Mi-2URP Salamandra light anti-tank helicopter with Malyutka missiles. The Polish People's Air Force, or Ludowe Lotnictwo Polskie, takes to the skies with the MiG-21 in an air defense or close air support role, backed by the Su-22M4 with either a rocket or anti-tank payload.

The 4 Dywizja Zmechanizowana, or 4th Mechanized Infantry Division, was originally formed in Ukraine by Polish communist forces in 1944. After World War II, the force was integrated into the new Polish People’s Army, or Ludowe Wojsko Polskie (LWP), and later reorganized as the 4th Mechanized "Pomeranian" Division. During the Cold War, the formation maintained full combat readiness, and in case of war, was destined to become part of the mobilized Polish 2nd Army, to see action against NORTHAG.

The Polish 4th Mechanized Infantry Division shares many similarities with its East German cousins in terms of equipment and organization, with the first-generation T-55 main battle tank as its workhorse, and the BWP-1 (BMP-1 in Polish service) as its primary IFV. Despite the Soviet-imposed uniformity, the LWP did field numerous domestic-made weapons and vehicles. Piechota, Komandosi, and Saperzy infantry either deploy with RPG-7VM or the indigenous RPG-76 Komar. The Czechoslovakian-Polish Skot is one of the main wheeled APCs, while the Star-266 is the first choice as a truck and prime mover. The upgraded T-55AM Merida, with its highly accurate fire-control system, is another example of a successful Polish design. Furthermore, Poland developed many variants of the lighter Mi-2 helicopter, including the W-3W Sokol.

The Korpus Desantowy was an amalgamation of Polish forces envisioned to spearhead the invasion of the outlying Danish islands in case of war, through a combined airborne and amphibious landing. The first phase of this Polish People’s Army assault was given to a mix of highly trained paratroopers of the 6 Brygada Powietrznodesantowa, or the 6th Airborne Brigade, and full combat-readiness naval infantry from 7 Brygadę Desantowa, the 7th Sea Landing Brigade. These would be backed by a follow-up wave from the 15 Dywizja Zmechanizowan, or 15th Mechanized Infantry Division.

The Korpus Desantowy is supported by the Polish People’s Navy with heavy PTS-M Zaop tracked amphibious supply vehicles, as well as the Mi-6 Zaop helicopter, and the TOPAS R-3M command unit. Infantry is the battlegroup’s strong suit, ranging from well-armed Spadochroniarze paratroopers, Desant. Saperzy squads, to Niebieski Berety naval infantry in a host of different variants, including one fielding flamethrowers. Support vehicles include TOPAS APCs mounting a SPG-9 recoilless rifle, ASU-85 light airborne tank destroyer, self-propelled 2S1M Morski Gozdzi, and the W-3RR Procjon recon helicopter. As befits an air assault formation, helicopter support is plentiful, from Mi-24D gunships to the W-3W Sokol. Polish air cover is likewise capable, with the MiG-21 9.12 and SU-22M4 available with various payloads, including SEAD, rocket, and napalm.

The Nationale Volksarmee’s 20. Motorisierte Schützendivision, or 20th Motorized Infantry Division, was on paper a mobilization division with older equipment and a largely reservist core. However, its tank regiment was to be formed from a T-72 training unit, giving this East German division a uniquely heavy punch.
As part of the 5. Armee, this motorized infantry division was to secure NATO’s Covering Force Area on the left flank of the northernmost Warsaw Pact spearhead against JUTLAND command. To clear enemy delaying forces in the region, the East German division was reinforced with several powerful independent units, among them additional Soviet heavy armor.

The 20. Motorisierte Schützendivision deploys a sizable force of Reservisten infantry squads with older weapons and turretless Res. BTR-60PA APCs. They are reinforced by VPB police and Forward Deployed Funkaufklärer in DHS Mi-24D. Artillery is plentiful, including the BM-21 Grad and SPW-50PK (MRF) mine-clearing vehicles. The formation’s main armored workhorses are the older KPZ T-55 and T-54AM tanks, supported by the more capable KPZ. T-72 in limited numbers.
The Soviet Army brings heavy-hitting tanks with the T-64A Obr. 83 and the rarer T-64AM. The formation has access to numerous anti-air defense units, such as the older KuB-M1, Shilka SPAAAG, and MT-LB Strela 10M, but is clearly deficient in helicopter gunships and air support.
Only the East German Luftstreitkräfte flies a limited number of Su-22M4 strike aircraft, MiG-21bis, and the MiG-23 in air superiority roles.

The East German 4. Motorisierte Schützendivision was created in the 1950s as part of the new communist Nationale Volksarmee. Stationed in Gotha and Erfurt, opposite Fulda, the well-trained and politically reliable East Germans would be heavily involved in any Warsaw Pact offensive across the Inner German Border. In wartime, the mechanized infantry formation, taking part in the first attacks on NATO territory, was to be reinforced by the NVA’s elite airborne troops, the Luftsturmregiment 40. 

The 4th Motorized uses either domestic equipment or export versions of Soviet Army materiel. This means older tanks, such as the T-55, upgraded T-55AM2 and T-55AM2B with its 9M117 Bastion gun-tube-fired guided missile. Infantry is a mix of cheap and resilient Motorisierte Schützen, Panzerjäger, and Pioneer squads, deployable in trucks, BTR-50PK and SPW-70 APCs, or SPZ BMP-1 IFVs. Elite East German paratroopers provide a handful of Airborne-capable Fallschirmjäger squads and the unique and secretive Fs-Einsatzgruppe and Fs-Sprengtaucher recon units. These saboteur squads, dressed as NATO troops, can perform False Flag operations. Helicopter forces are highly capable, with the Mi-8 and Mi-24 available in a range of rocket-pod, anti-tank, or gunship variants.
The East German Luftstreitkräfte fields older and cheaper MiG-21Bis, bolstered by MiG-23BN strike aircraft and MiG-23MF fighter-bombers. This air force is supplemented by more modern MiG-29A and Su-22M4P SEAD aircraft.

The 7. Panzerdivision was formed in 1956 with the birth of the communist Nationale Volksarmee. Like other East German formations, this armored division was modeled along Soviet Army lines, but dependent on domestic or export-variant equipment, some of it sourced from neighboring Warsaw Pact nations. In war, the 7th Armored Division would likely attack across the Inner German Border in a southwestern direction.

The 7th Armored counts on well-trained soldiers but has to make do with older, less sophisticated weaponry. The core of the formation’s firepower is clustered around the basic T-72 “mobilization tank”, backed by the more capable T-72M and T-72M1. First-generation T-55A plus T-55AK command tanks, and SPW-40P2 Konkurs ATGM carriers complement this armored fist. Supporting infantry are limited in number, ranging from Pioneer combat engineers with flamethrowers, PKM, and automatic grenade launcher weapon teams to Motorisierte Schützen deployable in either SPW-70 APCs or BMP-1 IFVs.
Czechoslovakian-made vehicles, including the heavy T813 supply truck and MFRW RM-70 rocket launcher, can also be deployed. Recon forces range from Aufkl.Pz. BRM-1s, Spezialaufklärer squads, and nimble Mi-2 helicopters.
The East German air force brings a mix of older MiG-21Bis and more modern MiG-23MF in either close air support or air defense roles. The capable Su-22M4 strike aircraft also takes to the sky.

The 9. Panzerdivision was the cream of the crop of the Nationale Volksarmee, well trained and lavishly equipped. Much like the rest of the communist East German army, the division was created at its inception in 1956. Being based in Eggesin, it was earmarked for duty in the 5th Army, which was to face NORTHAG in case of war. The armored division was not only the sole NVA formation completely outfitted with the T-72, but also the solitary user of the BMP-2 in East German service.

The 9. Panzerdivision’s tanks are all variants of the T-72, available in significant numbers, including the KPz T-72M1, the T-72MUV2, and the most recent main Soviet export variant, the T-72S. Mechanized infantry ride to battle in BMPs, such as the regular SPz BMP-1, plus a new variant equipped to fire the Konkurs ATGM, as well as the more capable but rarer SPz BMP-2, transporting a Motorisierte Schützen squad fielding the state-of-the-art RPG-27. Some other notable units include the heavy T813 supply truck, which also forms the basis of the RM-70/85 napalm-firing MLRS, the Schimmwagen MAV amphibious jeep, and the GF Shturm-S Kokon-firing tank destroyer. The East German Luftstreitkräfte provides ample ground support to the division, with a mix of Su-22M4 fighter-bombers and MiG-23 fighters.

The Berliner Gruppierung, or Berlin Grouping, was an amalgamated battlegroup centered on the East German 1. Motorisierte Schützendivision. Arrayed around West Berlin, this force is supported by artillery and combat engineers, border guards, military police, and special forces. In wartime, it was tasked with eliminating the NATO enclave deep behind the lines as part of Unternehmen Zentrum (Operation Center).

The Berliner Gruppiering specializes in high-intensity urban warfare and has a well-equipped logistical train, from MT-LBs to Mi-8T supply helicopters. Infantry range from Motorisierte Schützen with Strela MANPADs to KdA militia, Pionier squads with AGI incendiary rocket launchers, and elite Stasi Wachschutzen. The division contains a wide range of older equipment, from T-55A tanks to the timeless T-34/85 and light ZiS-2 57mm AT gun. Artillery is well represented, from 120mm mortars to SFL-H 2S1 122mm and D-20 152mm howitzers. Not letting any piece of equipment go to waste, the dual-purpose World War II-era ZiS-3 and M-30 towed guns get a second lease of life. Anti-air defenses are formidable with plentiful Fla-Sfl 23-4 Shilka and long-range 2K12 Kub. Air focuses on ground support aircraft fitted out with rocket and napalm payloads. These include the capable Su-22M4, MiG-21Bis light bomber, and the cheap L-39ZO trainer. Not close to the front, fighter cover is limited to MiG-23ML fighters.

The Kampfgruppen der Arbeiterklasse Bezirk Erfurt, or Erfurt District’s Combat Group of the Working Class, was an East German reserve force made up of citizen soldiers and paramilitary units. This defensive formation, equipped with an arsenal of mothballed materiel, was to be used to secure the Warsaw Pact’s rear and protect vital military sites and friendly heavy corps assets such as artillery and anti-air units.

K.d.A. Bezirk Erfurt calls on especially large KdA militia squads, fielding older small arms, with additional Sicherungs, Militarstreifen, and Soviet Zagradotryad military police, as well as Reservisten deployable in BTR-152 and BTR-50 APCs. The divisional logistical base is generous, including the heavy M-26 supply helicopter. Artillery is likewise well-regarded, from M-46 130mm howitzers to the super-heavy 2S7M Malka. Various MLRS systems can also unleash their devastating rocket payloads, such as the venerable heavy BM-24M, the BM-21 with its Napalm warheads, and the Cluster-equipped BM-30 Smerch. Anti-air units include the ZSU-57-2 SPAAG and long-range 9K37 Buk-M1. With much of the division’s equipment being older-generation, or even obsolete, armored forces have to make do with T-54Bs and a smattering of T-62s, PT-76s, including a recon version, and museum-worthy T-34/85M tanks. Fixed-wing air support is divided between Soviet and East German air forces, from rocket-wielding MiG-21bis to anti-tank MiG-27M, the SEAD Su-24MP, and MiG-23MF fighters.

The Rügener Gruppierung, or Rügener Grouping, took its name from Rügen Island, on the East German Baltic Coast, the location of the main communist Volksmarine naval base. To defend this critically important site, a substantial Nationale Volksarmee garrison was in place, the Besondere Gruppierung II (Special Grouping II). In war, the formation was to be bolstered by reservists, troops in training, and allied Polish units. The amalgamated battlegroup was also to secure the nearby Sassnitz ferry port, through which much of the USSR's strategic military supply entered East Germany. 

The mixed East German and Polish Rügener Gruppierung contains various mobilized detachments and formations under a single unified command. These include East German Marinepionier squads backed by Reservisten, Vopos militia, and Polish Piechota Zmech. infantry deployable in STAR-266 trucks or TOPAS-2A APCs. Supporting combat arms are plentiful, including the short-range mine-clearing SPW-50PK(MRF) MRLS, the SPW-40P recon armored car, large amphibious Schwimmwagen PTS-M tracked supply vehicle, towed PAK K-52 85mm, East German scout-engineer recon diver squads, and even elite KSK special forces. Other supporting units include the Mi-8TB helicopter and its rare Mi-14PL anti-ship variant, the Flak KS-19M2 100mm AA gun, Fasta-4 SAM, and the massive 2K11M3 Krug-M3. Air cover is likewise potent, from the nimble Polish LiM-6M to the MiG-23BN [KMGU] with its anti-personnel cluster bombs.

The West German 1. Luftlandedivision, or the 1st Air Landing Division, was raised in 1956, a year after the Bundeswehr’s founding. The initial deployment saw the formation’s use as a strategic reserve dispersed among the three main West German corps. At the tail end of the Cold War, the Bundeswehr consolidated most of the division in the Bavarian south, bolstered by the Gebirgsjägerbrigade 23 and territorial troops of the well-armed Heimatschutzbrigade 56.

The 1. Luftlandedivision contains a well-trained cadre of Airborne- and Mountaineer-traited infantry, from Forward Deployable Fallschirmjäger to Gebirgsjäger and elite Hochgebirgsjäger, backed by various helicopters and Airliftable transports. They excel at fighting in rough terrain. This expertise is extended to recon units, with large Gebirgsjäger Aufklärer and Jagdkommando troops deploying side-by-side with Fallschirmjäger B1 commandos. Vehicles range from Marder 1A1 IFVs, a rare Leopard 1A1A2, and Aufkl. Leopard 1A5 recon tank, and the reservist-manned M48A2GA2. The light Italian-made FS-M56 105mm howitzer, designed explicitly for mountainous warfare, can also be deployed, as well as the fast CL-289 recon drone and truck-mounted Unimog S404 FK-20 anti-air. Located near the Wehrtechnische Dienststelle 61, the Bundeswehr's technical center for aircraft improvement, a variety of exotic testbed planes can be used, from F-4F with laser-guided bombs, Tornado IDS in SEAD variant, the HFB-320/ECM electronic warfare aircraft, to the nimble Alpha Jet A KWS with anti-tank missiles.

The 2. Panzergrenadier-Division was one of the Bundeswehr’s founding formations in 1956. As part of the West German III Corps, the mechanized infantry division served in the northern reaches of CENTAG. Based in Kassel, it constituted a vital link between NATO’s strategic commands. In war, additional support would come from a Belgian recon regiment and RAF air cover.

The 2. Panzergrenadier-Division relies on mechanized infantry fighting in close cooperation with tanks. Some of the most modern West German armored vehicles are available to support the Panzergrenadier squads, from the Marder IFV to the Leopard 2A3 main battle tank. Airborne infantry can Forward Deploy as lightly equipped Fallschirmjäger squads, recon, and weapon teams. Belgian recon units include Eclaireurs scouts and British-made CVR(T) vehicle series, such as the Scimitar light tank, Spartan APC, and Striker ATGM carrier. Artillery and anti-air units are powerful and plentiful, including the LARS 2 MLRS, towed I-Hawk, and Gepard 1A1 SPAAGs. The skies above are protected by a mix of Luftwaffe, Belgian Air Force, and RAF Germany planes. The West Germans field Phantom F-4F and Tornado strike aircraft in various configurations, the Belgians F-16 fighters and Mirage 5BA tactical bombers, while the British provide Harrier GR.3, as well as their Tornado F.3 and GR.1 in air superiority and SEAD variants.

The Bundeswehr’s 5. Panzerdivision was assigned to III Corps, located in the north of CENTAG. As part of the founding of the new West German army in 1956, the armored division was based in Hesse. In war, the division’s panzers would have played an important role in containing Warsaw Pact forces before counterattacking the communists in the region north of Fulda.

The 5. Panzerdivision’s tank arsenal is formidable and includes not only a large contingent of older Leopard 1A1A1 and Leopard 1A5, but also the Jaguar 1 and 2 ATGM carriers, the modern Leopard 2A3, and its most heavily armored and advanced variant, the Leopard 2A4. The West German formation counts on Panzergrenadier mechanized infantry, as well as Sicherungs and Jäger squads, deployable in soft-skin vehicles, Marder IFVs, and M113A1Gs. Recon contains Alouette II helicopters and Fernspaher special forces. Artillery features both towed and self-propelled options, such as Panzermorser mortar carriers, MARS rocket artillery, and FH155-1 howitzers. The Gepard 1A1, along with the Roland 2 and 3 SAM systems, provides a deadly anti-air shield. In the skies above, the Luftwaffe fields the F-4F in anti-tank, rocket, tactical bomber, and air superiority roles. The modern Tornado IDS strike aircraft, in various close air support variants, can also be deployed, including one with the destructive anti-infantry cluster MW-1 dispenser.

The West German 6. Panzergrenadier-Division's primary task was to defend the Schleswig-Holstein region of West Germany as part of NATO’s LANDJUT, on the border with Denmark.
To help resist for as long as possible, allowing additional NATO reinforcements to deploy to this theater, the 6. Panzergrenadier was one of the largest Bundeswehr formations, heavily reinforced by Heimatschutzbrigade 51, a territorial army brigade, a helicopter regiment, and even Bundesmarine units from local naval bases.

The 6. Panzergrenadier is a hybrid division sitting between a mechanized and armored Bundeswehr formation, but lacking some of the most modern or heavy-hitting equipment. The battlegroup’s Panzergrenadier, some of which were trained for air assaults, as well as Heimat. Jäger squads are numerous. However, only older variants of the Leopard 1, including the 1A1A2 and 1A2A1, can be deployed.Other noteworthy units include the CL-89 UAV, the Bofors L/70 MFG, and the FRR Roland MFG anti-air SAM.
West German Navy support is plentiful, bringing a slew of naval infantry units, from assault engineer Strandmeister, to Marinesicherungs squads and Kampfschwimmer special forces.
The West German Navy’s air branch, the Marineﬂiegergeschwader, brings Sea King helicopters and the Do-28D-2 unarmed recon plane. They likewise lend a much-needed hand with their Tornado MFG in Cluster and SEAD loadouts. and F-104G MFG in fighter-bomber roles can also take to the skies. Danish F-16A provide key air cover for their West German allies.

Territorialkommando Süd, meaning Territorial Command South, covered a host of West German rear-area and reserve troops stationed in CENTAG and SOUTHAG. A handful of allied NATO units supported this division-sized battlegroup. These second-line forces would be first responders to sabotage or airborne operations, or used as a last-ditch effort to contain Warsaw Pact breakthroughs.

Territorialkommando Süd has an excellent logistical base with its MAN Kat 6x6, UH-1D and CH-53G helicopter supply units. Cheap and numerous are its infantry, from Jäger squads to Heimatschützen, Feldjäger military police, and MILAN ATGMs with their MTW M113A1G MILAN transports. NATO support comes as elite American Green Berets, French heliborne Aeromobiles squads, recon AMX-10 RC, and Gazelle helicopters. Territorialkommando Süd has to make do with West German tank reserves, chiefly the old M48A2CGA1 and A2 variants, plus Kanonenjagdpanzer. Artillery contains the Hs.30 Panzermorser and the long-range M110A2 203mm howitzer. Much more powerful is the division’s anti-air defenses, ranging from towed Flak L/70 Bofors 40mm and I-Hawk to the self-propelled Roland 2 and 3 SAMs. The divisional air cover is best described as a flying circus of older Luftwaffe aircraft, from museum-worthy GINA G.91R/3 to Alpha Jet trainers and reserve F-104Gs, with a few more capable French Mirage 2000C RDI fighters and American F-111F LGB variants in support.

The Soviet 119-y Odtelniy Tankoviy Polk, or 119th Independent Tank Regiment, was stationed in Bad Langensalza, East Germany. This type of second-echelon formation served as an exploitation force, projected to advance deep into NATO’s operational rear once a breakthrough had been achieved. In the case of a Fulda Gap offensive, this armored spearhead of the Soviet 8th Guards Army was to form the core of a small Operational Maneuver Group with an engineer brigade and recon regiment attached.

The battlegroup calls on the most fearsome and advanced of the Soviet main battle tanks: the heavily armored T-80UD and the earlier T-80U. The T-80BVK command tanks provide local leadership, while TO-55 flamethrower tanks and Rapira towed anti-tank guns add extra firepower. The very destructive TOS-1 Buratino short-range thermobaric rocket launcher can also deploy. The Soviet armored force might be formidable, but its supporting arms - from logistics to infantry - are limited. Infantry consists of a handful of Spetsnaz special forces and Saperi combat engineers. Artillery and anti-air units are likewise constrained, with only a few self-propelled 2S1 Gvozdika and towed 2A65 Msta-B 152mm howitzers, 2K22 Tugunska SPAAGs, and MT-LB Strela-10 SAM units. Helicopter and air forces are capable, with a good deal of Mi-24V attack helicopters backed by MiG-29 and Su-27S fighters, and Su-24M strike aircraft with various loadouts.

The Soviet 157-ya Motostrelkovaya Diviziya, or 157th Motor Rifle Division, was based in the Crimea, protecting the vitally important Black Sea Fleet bases near Sevastopol. A mobilization division with only a limited cadre of professional soldiers during peacetime, the defensive formation was first raised in 1969. As part of the Soviet Army’s 32nd Army Corps, the division’s reservists would have absorbed nearby training units, as well as Soviet Navy assets, in times of armed conflict.

The 157th fields a small force of regular Motostrelki squads, supported in significant numbers by Rezervisiti relying on older BTR-152K and BTR-40 APCs. Fielding a museum-worthy quantity of older small arms are the truck-borne Partizani squads, backed by some equally ancient IS-2M tanks taken out of mothballs. Slightly more modern armor are T-54B and T-55As, but most of the support arms stem from World War II, including BS-3 100mm anti-tank guns, D-1 152mm howitzers, BM-24M MLRS, and the super-heavy B-4M 203mm and Br-5M 280mm artillery behemoths. Naval and coastal defense units include K-1 recon helicopters, the state-of-the-art A222 Bereg 130mm self-propelled artillery, and the KSM-65 100mm towed anti-tank gun. Air support comes in the form of the older Su-15TM interceptor and the T-10K, a navalised Su-27K flown by Soviet Navy pilots.

The 17-ya Gvardeyskaya Tankovaya Diviziya, or 17th Guards Tank Division, was, despite its renowned “Guard” designation, a low-readiness mobilization division based in the Ukrainian SSR. With only a skeleton crew, this second-echelon division would rapidly muster its reserve forces upon war. The 17th Guards would likely be directed into nearby Czechoslovakia, scooping up a host of army-level attachments before entering the fray. 

The 17th Guards Tank Division concentrates all of the remaining early-production T-64R main battle tanks, further backed by a sizable contingent of World War II-era ISU-152K self-propelled guns and even more numerous T-10M, the ultimate specimen of the post-war Iosef Stalin-series of heavy tanks. A handful of regular Motostrelki squads are supplemented by Rezervisti and Pogranvoiska KGB border guards, including recon variants, deployed near the USSR’s internal frontier with Czechoslovakia. Several East German and Polish pieces of equipment have also found their way into this battlegroup, such as the reservist-manned ML-20 152mm howitzers, the BM-14M MRLS, the self-propelled 2S7M Malka, and the 2S4 Tyulpan super-heavy 240mm mortar, plus the ZSU-23-4M1 Shilka SPAAG. The division’s air cover is provided by the MiG-23ML and the longer-range MLA variant, with an all-out air-fleet of Su-17M4 providing close air support, including with Thermobaric and combined HE and CLU payloads.

The Soviet Army’s 25-ya Tankovaya Diviziya, or the 25th Tank Division, saw the light after World War II’s conclusion, being destined for garrison duty in Soviet-occupied Germany. Based in East German Vogelsang, near the Polish border, the armored division was part of the 20th Guards Combined Army. As a powerful follow-up force, it would have been used to exploit any communist breakthrough into the North German Plains. 

The 25th Tank Division, unlike any other Soviet Army formation, is not only fully equipped with state-of-the-art T-64 main battle tanks but also features four instead of three tank regiments. The unusual lack of an infantry regiment means that only a limited number of Motostrelki and Saperi squads will be available. The battlegroup’s tank force is formidable, with a whole arsenal of T-64B, B1, and older T-64A Obr. 83, with variants differing in fire control systems, ERA, armor, or the ability to fire anti-tank guided missiles. The T-64B1 Razv. can be deployed as a potent recon tank, with the Schmel-1 UAV watching from the sky above. Some heavy self-propelled artillery, courtesy of the 34th Artillery Division, can deploy, including the long-range 2S5 Giatsint-S and the brand-new 2S19 Msta-S.

The 27-ya Gvardeyskaya Motostrelkovaya Diviziya, or the 27th Guards Motor Rifle Division, was earmarked in 1989 to be the next-generation Soviet Army formation. Designated a testbed for the “Division ‘90” concept, a number of cutting-edge weaponry was introduced by the Group of Soviet Forces Germany. However, looming conflict in Europe limited the round of experimentation to this single modernized combined-arms division.

The 27th Guards has access to some of the latest hardware to be deployed in the Soviet Army. Motostrelki and Saperi squads feature new camouflage uniforms, RPG-26 and RPG-27 rocket launchers, while Spetsrazvedka recon squads, Otdelenie Podderzhki tank hunters, and Konkurs-M ATGM teams can also deploy. The state-of-the-art BMP-3 is available as an IFV, supported by T-80BV armor. The wheeled BRDM-2 Konkurs-M and the hard-hitting but short-range towed 2A45M Sprut-B provide additional anti-tank firepower. Artillery is modern, from the 2S12 120mm mortar to the wheeled 2S23 Nona-SVK, towed 2A36 Giatsint-B 152mm howitzer, and precision-guided artillery shells of the upgraded 2S3M1 Akatsiya. Anti-air is likewise potent, including the Strela-10M3 and 9K330 Tor systems. The Soviet Air Forces deploy the Su-17M4 attack aircraft, MiG-23MLD and MiG-29 fighters, and the next-generation close-support plane, the T-8M, bristling with Vikhr anti-tank missiles.

The Soviet 2-ya Tamanskaya Gvardeyskaya Motostrelkovaya Diviziya, or 2nd Guards Tamanskaya Motorized Rifle Division, was a prestigious formation protecting the capital of the USSR. Beginning its life as the 127th Rifle Division in 1940, the unit saw extensive action during the Great Patriotic War, becoming one of the most famous and decorated formations in the Red Army, even attaining the Guards and Tamanskaya honorifics. In the late Cold War, the Moscow-based division was highly trained and lavishly equipped. Officers were handpicked for their loyalty, as this formation was envisioned not only to guard against foreign attacks but also domestic threats, including rebellions. 

The 2nd Guards can call upon some of the latest models of tanks and air superiority fighters available to the Soviet Army, with its Gvardeitsy infantry squads fielding their own type of uniform and small arms. As a mechanized infantry division, it follows the standard communist template of motorized Motostrelki squads backed by a sizable main battle tank contingent. Armor includes the T-72A Obr. 83 main battle tank and a handful of the state-of-the-art T-80U obr. 1989 with Kontakt-5 ERA. Other special units include SIGINT-capable R-330 RAMA trucks, recon Razv BTR-80 APCs, while patrolling the capital’s skies are the ground-strike MiG-23P aircraft, Su-15TM interceptors, and advanced MiG-29 9.13 fighters.

The Soviet 31-ya Tankovaya Diviziya, or the 31st Tank Division, was the direct successor to the World War II-era 31st Tank Corps of the Red Army, a formation that ended the war in Czechoslovakia. Reorganized and reformed, the division was stationed in nearby Hungary before taking part in the Warsaw Pact’s intervention during the Prague Spring of 1968. Afterwards, the tank division remained in eastern Czechoslovakia for the duration of the Cold War, subordinated to the Soviet Central Group of Forces. 

The 31st Tank Division can deploy a wide array of capable Soviet Army units, from the massive Mi-22 command helicopter to a large number of the sprawling T-72 tank family, with the T-72A obr. 79 being the mainstay, to the 9A51 Prima, a heavier variant of the Grad-based MRLS system. The battlegroup can also count on a large contingent of Czechoslovakian troops to bolster its ranks in the field, including Střelci infantry and ATGM weapon teams, RM Vz.51 130mm MLRS, H D-30 122mm howitzers, and self-propelled Ještěrka twin 30mm SPAAG. A curious recon unit is the BMAN, a rocket-wielding spotting vehicle featuring one of the few advanced Electro-Optical Dazzler systems in Soviet service.

The 35-ya Gvardeyskaya Desantno-Shturmovaya Brigada, or the 35th Guards Air Assault Brigade, traced its origins to the late 1940s. Part of the VDV (Soviet Airborne Forces), it was trained and specifically equipped for air assaults. Briefly deployed to Afghanistan, the formation was transferred to East Germany, where it became the 35th Guards Air Assault Brigade. In wartime, the VDV would attack key strategic points or conduct operations behind enemy lines.

The 35th Guards Air Assault features a mix of trained Desantniki, veteran Afgantsy, and Spetsnaz squads with Forward Deployment and follow-up infantry deploying in Mi-2 and Mi-8T helicopters. Uniquely for an air assault formation, it is highly mechanized, relying on the heavily armed but lightly armored BMD and BRT-series, also sporting the Airborne trait. These include the BMD-1 and -2, anti-tank BRT-RD Robot, anti-air BTR-D Skrezhet, and recon 1V119 Reostat. Tanks are non-existent, with most of the supporting arms made up of light and specialized units, ranging from 2B9 Vasilek automatic mortar and self-propelled 2S9 Nona, to the BM-21V Grad-V MRLS, towed ZU-23-2 23mm, and D-44 85mm anti-tank guns. Heliborne support is substantial, from the recon Mi-24K to the advanced but rare Ka-50 attack helicopter. Air cover comprises the MiG-27 bomber in various loadouts, the MiG-25BM SEAD and MiG-25RBF bombers, and the MiG-23ML and MiG-29 fighters.

The Soviet 39-ya Gvardeyskaya Motostrelkovaya Diviziya, or the 39th Guards Motorized Rifle Division, began its illustrious career in Stalingrad’s Red October steelworks in 1942, ending victorious at Berlin’s Brandenburg Gate in 1945. A permanent readiness division based in East Germany, it was part of the Soviet 8th Guards Army. In war, this well-equipped division was to spearhead the Warsaw Pact’s offensive through the Fulda Gap.

As a motorized rifle division, the 39th Guards was to break through heavily defended sectors during combined-arms operations. Regular Motorstrelki infantry and Saperi assault squads deploy with a variety of weapons and vehicles, including RPG-7V and RPG-22 anti-tank rockets, short-range Metis ATGMs, wheeled BTR-60s, or tracked BMP-1 and BMP-2 IFVs. A sizable number of T-80B and T-80BV provide armored back-up, further supported by long-range MT-LB Shturm-S ATGM carriers. Radzveka scouts, deploying alongside East German Grenzer border troops and recon helicopters, provide battlefield intel. The 2S3M Akatsiya and BM-27 Uragan MLRS, plus the 9K33M3 OSA-AKM and 2K12 Kub SAM systems, are some of the self-propelled artillery and anti-air units available. Helicopter support is powerful with Mi-8 and well-armed Mi-24 gunships. Air cover is likewise potent, from the slow-flying but armored Su-25 to Su-24 strike aircraft, East German Su-22M4 and MiG-23MF tactical bombers, MiG-27K equipped with laser-guided bombs, and MiG-23MLD and Su-27S fighters.

The Soviet 56-ya Otdel’naya Gvardeyskaya Desantno-Shturmovaya Brigada, or 56th Separate Guards Air Assault Brigade, had a history that was closely tied to the Soviet-Afghan War of the 1980s. The particular VDV battlegroup was created from several independent units, and only two months after its inception, it took part in the initial invasion of Afghanistan. In time, the Soviet brigade became closer to a mechanized infantry formation, using BMP-2s and additional firepower of T-62 tanks. With conflict in Europe on the horizon, the experienced 56th Separate Guards Air Assault Brigade was transferred to East Germany, to be an integral part of the Warsaw Pact’s offensive plans against NATO.

The 56th Separate Guards Air Assault Brigade fields some of the most battle-hardened airborne veterans of the Soviet Army, backed by a series of unique battlefield-modified vehicles. These range from Spetsnaz GRU (Stinger) special forces equipped with looted NATO weapons to lightly armed Okhrana squads with RPO Rys and RPG-16 rocket launchers. Improvised units include the ZSU-23-4M2 (PSNR), an anti-air SPAAG converted for ground surveillance, the LuAZ amphibious jeeps, a variety of wheeled BTR-70 and tracked GM-TU vehicles, and the super-heavy towed M-240 mortar. In the skies above, the Mi-8PPA jamming helicopter and Mi-24P gunships are joined by the MiG-27, which provides potent anti-tank air support.

The Soviet 6-ya Gvardeyskaya Motostrelkovaya Brigada, or 6th Guards Separate Motor Rifle Brigade, was the Warsaw Pact counterpart to the NATO garrisons stationed in West Berlin. Formed after the Berlin Crisis of 1962, it protected the communist East Berlin, providing military police and ceremonial troops. However, in times of conflict, reinforced for the Warsaw Pact’s offensive Unternehmen Zentrum plans, the formation would spearhead the assault on the city from within its tight urban confines.

The 6th Guards battlegroup counts on a host of experienced infantry, mostly Soviet Motostrelki and Saperi squads, Komendatura military police, backed by East German Vopos militia and Motorisierte Schützen in BMPs. Several special forces and paratrooper squads are also available, including East German Luftsturm-Jäger squads transportable in armed Mi-2 and Mi-8 helicopters, and the KGB’s elite Spetsgruppa “A” saboteur squads with their False Flag trait and civilian attire. The capable T-64 tanks, including the upgraded T-64B variant, provide some much-needed armor support, while artillery forces can deploy the long-range 2S5 Giantsint-S and powerful BM-27 Urugan MRLS. This far from the front, patrolling the skies against enemy intruders and bombers rests on the shoulders of the Soviet Air Defence Forces’ long-range MiG-31M interceptor. Other aircraft include the L-39ZO trainer, which also doubles up as a light bomber.

The Soviet 76-ya Gvardiyska Vozdushno-Desantnaya Diviziya, or 76th Guards Airborne Division, traced its lineage back to the Red Army’s 157th Rifle Division of World War II. The parent division fought with distinction in various epic battles, from Stalingrad to Kursk, Operation Bagration, and the Battle of Berlin. After the war, it was reformed as a Soviet airborne division, part of the VDV, specifically equipped for air assault missions. With World War III looming in Europe, the well-trained division would have had the unenviable task of destroying the French nuclear weapons in a high-risk Warsaw Pact mission deep in enemy territory. 

The 76th Guards Airborne Division counts on a significant proportion of its troops going to battle in light but highly advanced equipment, including the state-of-the-art BMD-3 armored vehicle in both tank and recon roles. Earlier generations of the BMD are also available, such as the BTR-D, ready to transport Desantniki, Desant. Sapery and large Desant. Usilennie VDV infantry squads. Other specialized units featured are the Desant. Gaz-66B SNAB supply truck, LuAZ Korrektirovschik artillery command unit, LuAZ 2F62 Zenitchik AA units, and Schmel-1 UAV for remote aerial recon. The Soviet Air Forces provide long-range aviation support in the form of newly equipped SU-24M, including one variant with powerful thermobaric bombs, and the fast MiG-31 air defense fighter.

The Soviet 79-ya Gvardeyskaya Tankovaya Diviziya, or the 79th Guards Tank Division, was forged in the flames of Stalingrad, before fighting its way through the Crimea, Poland, East Prussia, and ultimately Berlin. Remaining in East Germany, the unit was reorganized as a tank division in 1965. A high-readiness formation, the 79th was one of the best-equipped and trained in the Group of Soviet Forces in Germany. In case of conflict, as part of the 8th Guards Army, it was planned to exploit any breakthrough in the Fulda Gap.

The 79th Guards calls on the mobility and firepower of the latest series of Soviet main battle tanks. As such, it fields the T-80BV with reactive armor, including a distinct variant with a supercharged engine, backed by earlier T-80Bs. Limited Motostrelki squads in wheeled APCs, BMP-1s, or BMP-2s IFVs provide infantry support. Recon forces include Spetznas G.R.U. and Razdvedka scout squads deployable in BMP-2s or rocket-armed helicopters. Self-propelled anti-air defenses are heavily employed, ranging from Strela-10M and heavy long-range Buk-M1 to state-of-the-art 2K22 Tunguska SPAAGs. The Soviet Air Forces are out for war, flying everything from the Su-25 in a variety of close-air support loadouts, to Su-24M tactical bombers, MiG-27K SEAD planes, and MiG-23ML and MiG-29 fighters for air superiority missions.

The Soviet 1-ya Gvardeyskaya Proletarskaya Motostrelkovaya Diviziya, or the 1st Guards Proletarian Motorized Infantry Division, was one of the longest-serving formations of the Soviet Army.
First formed in 1926 from various independent and training battalions in the Moscow region, it was destroyed and reformed at least once during World War II.
It ended in 1945 near Königsberg, East Prussia, having attained the esteemed Guards status.

Based in the Kaliningrad Oblast as part of the Baltic Military District, the reduced combat-ready division’s role would have been to be mobilized quickly and used as a second echelon of any strategic war offensive.
Rushed to the front, and reinforced by several anti-tank formations, the division would have arrived in the East German Magdeburg area just in time to repel NATO’s surprise counter-attack.

The 1st Guards Proletarian Division was among the first Soviet Army divisions to receive early versions of the T-72, though these were never upgraded during the Cold War. As such, the division features the up-armored T-72 Ural-1 and the T-72AV fitted with ERA. The radar-guided towed MT-12R Ruta 100mm anti-tank gun can also deploy, as well as the advanced long-range MT-LB Ataka ATGM tank destroyer./nOther noteworthy units include the R-330T Taran SIGINT vehicle, the rare Pero UAV, MiG-25PD interceptors, and the retro-looking YaK-28PP Electronic Warfare airplane.

The Soviet 336-ya Otdel’naya Gvardeyskaya Brigada Morskoy Pekhoty, or the 336th Separate Guards Naval Infantry Brigade, was one of the Soviet Navy’s elite amphibious assault formations. The Soviet marines earned their “Black Death” nickname for their black uniforms and their stubbornness in World War II combat.
The small Baltic Fleet formation, based in Kaliningrad since 1963, required mobilization to attain full war strength. The Soviet Navy deployed specialized variants of standard armored vehicles, including amphibious ones. The Soviet naval infantrymen of the 336th Guards Naval Infantry would most likely see action against the Nordic countries, specifically Denmark, in an effort to secure the crucial Baltic Straits.

The 336th Guards Naval Infantry deploys an arsenal of specialized vehicles, chiefly to support the Morpekhi naval infantry squads, some of which are trained in air assault, and come in a variety of different sizes, including Rezervisti, Komroti command, and Spetsnaz. Specialized naval infantry weaponry include the Mor. 2S9-1 Sviristelka with additional ammo, Mi-14PL recon helicopters, BM-21-1 Grad on a Zil-131 chassis, and the amphibious PTS-2 supply barge.
The Soviet Navy also deployed the advanced T-55AMD main battle tanks with the Drodz active protection system, further backed by long-range T-55AM with Bastion ATGMs. The heavy Tu-22 in a carpet bomber role and the Tu-22KDP electronic warfare variant can be flown as air support.

The 94-ya Gvardeyskaya Motostrelkovaya Diviziya, or the 94th Guards Motorized Rifle Division, was based on the very northern edge of the Group of Soviet Forces in Germany, overlooking the East German shores of the Baltic Sea. Tasked with driving northwest across the West German frontier region into Denmark and creating a springboard for the subsequent 1st Polish Army to attack Jutland, this division was heavily reinforced for breakthrough attacks and equipped with some of the best the Soviet Army could muster.
One of the first to convert to the potent T-64 main battle tank, the 94th Guards’ equipment and organisation started to show its age by 1989. 

The 94th Guards Motorized Rifle Division deploys numerous Motostrelki mechanized infantry and Saperi combat engineers, along with unarmed Potok-2 command IFVs, PTS-2 amphibious carriers, and UR-67 mine-clearing vehicles. Earlier variants of the capable T-64 make up the division’s armored fist, such as the T-64A Obr. 81, T-64A Obr. 84, and T-64AV with reactive armor.
Other noteworthy units found with the 94th Guards are the MT-12R Ruta anti-tank gun with radar guidance, the IRM Jouk, an amphibious engineering BMP, as well as the Tu-143 Reys UAV and lightly armed Mi-8TARK recon units.

The Spanish División Mecanizada «Brunete» n.º 1, or Armoured Division No. 1 "Brunete", was created by the Franco regime in 1943, and named after an important Nationalist-won battle of the Spanish Civil War. When a newly democratic Spain joined NATO in 1982, the tank division was considered one of the best-armed of the Ejército de Tierra. In case of hostilities, it was to quickly reinforce SOUTHAG in West Germany. 

The Armoured Division No. 1 "Brunete" is a small formation with only two brigades, fielding a mix of domestic, French, and American equipment. The main battle tank is a Spanish AMX-30 variant with a light coaxial machine gun. Infantry come as Fusileros or Zapadores squads, deployable in Pegaso trucks, Santana PA jeeps, tracked TOA (M113), or the 6x6 wheeled BMR APC family. Part of the Brigada de Caballería “Jarama” I regiment is attached, bringing excellent recon forces, from Francotiradores snipers to wheeled VEC-25 and VEC-90 armored vehicles, plus the recon AMX-30EMI tank. Anti-air includes AMX-30RE SPAAG, Apside Toledo towed SAMs, and various gun platforms. The Ejército del Aire provides excellent air support with three types of aircraft: the C.12 (American F-4C) used in a ground attack role; the C.14A (French Mirage F1) as a bomber and fighter; and the C.15 (American F-18) in AT or air defense roles.

The Spanish División Mecanizada «Guzmán el Bueno» n.º 2, or Mechanised Division No.2 "Guzmán el Bueno", was one of the largest formations in the Spanish Army during the closing years of the Cold War. Based in southern Andalucia and named after a Spanish noble and hero during medieval times, it was envisioned to either deploy rapidly against potentially belligerent African nations or support NATO allies if conflict arose in West Germany.
