Mechanized by name, but motorized by nature, the battlegroup would be further reinforced by a variety of corps assets upon its call to action. 

The "Guzmán el Bueno" relies on smaller, infantry squads transported in a wide array of BMR APC variants, further supported by the light M47E2 and the more capable M48A5E2 tanks. Guerilleros recon special forces can deploy ahead of the main infantry, consisting of Fusileros and Zapadores squads. Additional corps assets include units such as the World War II-vintage Cañón 122/45 (Ruso .31), the L-10D3 300mm MLRS, Teleoka Electronic Warfare ground vehicles, and heavy C-3464 logistic trucks. UH-1H Mamee helicopter gunships provide local air cover, while the Ejército del Aire operates export variants of the Mirage III (C.11 in Spanish service) and Mirage F1 (C.14) in a variety of close air support and air defense roles.

The British 1st Armoured Division’s insignia was a testament to its tapestried military history, combining the rhinoceros of its World War II namesake and the red-bordered triangle of the 1st Division. Permanently stationed near the Inner German Border, the late Cold War-era “heavy” 1st Armoured Division was part of the British Army of the Rhine. The NORTHAG-based tank and anti-tank forces, together with airborne reserves from the British Isles, would contain and then counter any Warsaw Pact offensive.

The 1st Armoured Division fields an extensive arsenal of British armored vehicles, from FV432 Command to Warrior IFVs, bringing Armoured Rifles and Gun Group mechanized infantry squads. Several Forward Deployed-capable Terriers Paras and weapon teams are also available. Tank forces include the modern Challenger I Mk.2 and Mk.3, backed by older Chieftain Mk.9 and Mk. 11s. Long-range ATGM carriers, the FV438 Swingfire and FV102 Striker, can also be fielded. FV101 Scorpion and the FV721 Fox, supported by Scout, Sniper, and elite 4-man SAS Patrol squads, make up its recon forces. Supporting arms include the self-propelled FV432 Mortar and FV433 Abbot 105mm howitzer and the anti-air Tracked Rapier. RAF Germany brings close air support Harriers and Jaguar GR.1s, as well as Tornado F.3 air defense and Tornado GR.1 strike aircraft.

The British 2nd Infantry Division had a checkered past, reformed and reconstituted various times throughout its almost two hundred years of existence. In 1983, a reorganization incorporated a light airmobile component. While assigned to the British Army on the Rhine, the 2nd Infantry Division was actually based in the United Kingdom. Earmarked for immediate deployment in case of conflict, the formation would reinforce NORTHAG and bolster the British I Corps as quickly as possible.

The 2nd Infantry Division favors mobility over armor. Infantry is a strong point, from rapid Airmobile troops and Airmobile Pioneers to numerous territorial reservist Terrier squads and weapon teams. Elite SAS commandos fielding AT-4 rocket launchers and Stinger AA missiles can wreak havoc behind enemy lines, while Motorized Airmobiles in Saxon APCs provide additional ground support, as do a few Armoured Rifles squads in Warrior IFVs.

A handful of Challenger I tanks, seconded from strategic reserves, are available. The only self-propelled artillery piece is the M107A2 175mm gun. Anti-air defenses range from Blowpipe and Javelin MANPAD teams to towed and Tracked Rapier units.
Gazelle and Lynx in various payload loadouts provide treetop-skimming helicopter support, while RAF Harrier and Jaguar in ground attack roles, Phantom F.3 fighters, and Tornado GR.1 strike aircraft protect the skies above.

The 4th Armoured Division boasted an illustrious military career, having taken part in notable conflicts ranging from the Battle of Waterloo to the Boer Wars, World Wars I and II. In the late 1970s, after a series of convoluted reorganizations, the 4th Armoured Division was designated a NORTHAG frontline formation in West Germany, as part of the British Army of the Rhine.

The 4th Armoured Division forms a missing link in the British Army of the late 1980s, in effect a mechanized infantry division fielding older armored equipment. Only second-generation Chieftain main battle tanks, including Mk. 6/2 and Mk.11 variants, are available. Likewise, the formation’s plentiful Assault Pioneers, Rifles, and Motorised Rifles squads ride to battle in softskins, FV432 armored vehicles, or light but fast Saxons APCs. The FV432 is further employed in command, cargo, anti-air SCAT, MILAN, and Wombat versions. Notable units include the venerable AEC Militant Mk.3 heavy supply truck, demolition charges-firing Centurion Mk.5 AVRE ROMOR courtesy of the Royal Engineer Armoured Squadron, radar-equipped Lynx AH.7 Chancellor and rocket-firing Gazelle AH.1 helicopters. The Royal Air Force deploys Jaguars and Phantoms with various loadouts, including the Jaguar GR.1A with HE bombs and overwing air-to-air missiles, and Phantom FGR.2 fighter-bombers with HE and Cluster payloads.

Berlin Command was composed of the various Allied garrisons present in the Cold War’s iconic West Berlin. The U.S. Berlin Brigade, the British Berlin Infantry Brigade, and the French Forces Françaises à Berlin were to provide military deterrence. Encircled on all sides, the multinational Berlin Command was hopelessly outnumbered and outgunned. Still, these local NATO forces, specialized in urban combat, aimed to make any Warsaw Pact attack on the city an extremely costly affair.

Berlin Command calls on a wide array of military police, infantry, assault troops, and combat engineers. Forces range from American elite PSSE-B recon squads to British ad-hoc RAF Rifles. The FV432 Rarden, with its 30mm autocannon, serves as a repurposed fire support vehicle. The French field the light 53T2 20mm for local AA, and the towed American M198 howitzer provides field artillery. Treaty-bound, the West Germans could only deploy police forces, such as SEK assault squads and Fr. Polizei-Reserve. Heavier armor includes the American M728 CEV and M1IP Abrams, the British Chieftain Mk.10, with its striking urban camouflage, and French AMX-13/90 and AMX-30Bs. Air assets are as varied as the ground units, including smuggled-in RAF Harrier jump jets and state-of-the-art F-117A Nighthawk stealth bombers with LGB capability. The large, high-speed French Mirage IV conducts SEAD and carpet-bombing missions.

The United Kingdom’s Home Defence Region London covered the British Army and Territorial units assigned to London during the Cold War. Acting as a capital garrison of sorts, it contained a hodgepodge of defensive units, with the nucleus formed by the Guards battalions of the 56th (London) Infantry Brigade. The formation was further backed by various reservist regiments, including detachments engaged in Northern Ireland, War Materiel Reserve, ceremonial artillery, training units, and even elite SAS counter-terror squads. 

The Home Defence Region London deploys a wide-ranging mix of personnel and equipment, from Guards squads in their redcoats and bearskins, airborne Territorial troops, to Rifles Patrol sections redeploying from Northern Ireland, and grey-clad SAS special forces. The FV1613 Humber armored car is available in great numbers and in various configurations, supported by Centurion Mk.13 tanks, heavy Chinook HC.1B helicopters, Bedford TM supply trucks, World War II-era QF 25-pdr 88mm artillery, L5 105mm guns, to several prototypes of the state-of-the-art AS.90 155mm self-propelled gun. Anti-air and air cover is formidable, from the modern Starstreak LML to the heavy Bloodhound Mk.2 SAM. A  handful of A.109A helicopters captured from the Argentinians during the Falklands War see renewed service, together with ancient Canberra bombers, Hawk T.1A trainers, Phantom FGR.2 in air defense roles, and Harrier GR.5 attack aircraft.

NATO’s MultiNational Airborne Division, or MNAD, was a late Cold War suggestion for a NORTHAG quick reaction force that never advanced beyond its proposal on paper. The limited strategic reserves of each of the national Corps were considered a risk in case of a communist offensive. With World War III on the horizon, the MNAD would see a fast-tracked revival, combining a variety of light units of the Belgian, Dutch, and West German detachments under unified British command. 

The flexible MNAD relies on the elite fighting forces of the British 5 Airborne Brigade, the West German 27. Luftlandebrigade, and the Belgian Para-Commando Regiment. Paratrooper squads, from West German Fs.-Jäger to British Paras and Belgian Para-Commando wield the Airborne and Shock traits and some of their respective armies’ best small arms. Other renowned infantry featured are the famous Ghurkas and the Dutch Mariniers naval infantry. Battlefield mobility is a premium, which results in almost non-existent armor, but plenty of Airlift-capable units. These include the ATMP vehicles, L16 81mm mortar with Cluster munition, Kraka with TOWs, West German Wiesel tankettes, and even the rapid LSV M2HB buggy. Its helicopter force is powerful from Scout AH.1 Helarm, Agusta A109BA HTPT, to large CH-53G and Chinook HC.1 transports. Air is likewise well supplied with Buccaneer bombers, Mirage 5BA fighter-bombers, and F-16A air superiority fighters.

The renowned U.S. 101st Airborne Division (Air Assault) was first raised in World War II as a paratrooper formation, jumping famously into combat during D-Day, Market Garden, and seeing action during the Battle of the Bulge. The 101st Airborne also took part in the Vietnam War, followed by a deep reorganization that resulted in an airmobile division with close integration of helicopters and air assault-capable infantry. The late Cold War saw only limited deployment of the “Screaming Eagles”, even as part of the US Army’s quick reaction force, the XVIII Airborne Corps.

The 101st Airborne is organized as a light infantry division, but with levels of training and standards above regular U.S. Army formations, as well as substantially more helicopters, including the 160th Special Operations Aviation Regiment (Airborne), the U.S. special forces’ helicopter wing. A handful of M11P Abrams tanks will come courtesy of the 194th Armored Brigade. The light combat formation fields a wide range of specialized equipment, from Aero-Rifles squads, Green Berets (ODA), elite Delta operators, to the quirky 6x6 Gama Goat and M274 Mule transports. Air support includes the heavily armed MH-47D Chinook, nimble AH-6H Little Bird, MH-60A DAPs, and AH-64A Apache ATAS helicopters, as well as EF-11A Raven Electronic Warfare planes and F-15C Eagles for air superiority.

The U.S. 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment “Blackhorse” was CENTAG’s tripwire, a screening force situated directly on the Inner German Border. With the outbreak of war, the regiment’s squadrons were to be reinforced with a few West German and American battalions, intent on holding back the Warsaw Pact for as long as possible. Manning outposts such as the famous OP Alpha, U.S. 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment “Blackhorse’s” wartime mission near the Fulda Gap would be near-sacrificial, with life expectancy counted in hours.

The 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment’s recon units are top-notch, from LRS special forces and M1025 Humvee AGL to West German radar-equipped Green Archer and light Bundesgrenzschutz border guards. One of the most impressive is the M1A1 ACAV recon tank. Much like its logistical train and supporting arms, the regiment’s mechanized infantry is expensive to deploy but includes Engineers and Dismounted Troopers. The cavalry’s armor is well represented, with M1A1 Abrams bringing their heavy tank guns to bear. Attack helicopters can likewise be deployed cheaply but are limited to the older AH-1F Cobra and the AH-1F C-Nite with TOW-2 missiles. Flying top cover is the F-16 Fighting Falcon in various loadouts, including the F-16CG with laser-guided bombs, while the fearsome A-10 Thunderbolt provides devastating close air support.

The U.S. 1st Cavalry Division was formed in 1921 as a horse cavalry unit and saw action in the Pacific Theatre during World War II, and later in the Korean War.
Remaining in East Asia, the formation was reformed into an air assault division and saw further service in Vietnam, including famously at the Battle of Ia Drang. In the late 1980s, the 1st Cavalry Division was based in the continental United States as a test-bed formation.

The division was to be ferried to a war-engulfed Europe as part of REFORGER, using local POMCUS depots with ready-to-roll equipment.
The formation’s hurried deployment in NATO’s Magdeburg Counterstrike, without its usual National Guard brigade, would see the division take temporary command of the British 4th Armoured Brigade to bolster its battlefield presence.

The 1st Cavalry Division, although a “light” American armored division, deploys some unique weapon systems. These include the M2 Bradley IFV in various configurations, such as the anti-air M2 Bradley BSFV, M3 Bradley CFV recon vehicles, the M3 ETAS with its electro-optical recon mast, as well as Cav. Troopers fireteams, the M109A2 (GLCP) firing laser-guided shells, the CQM-121A Pave Tiger Electronic Warfare drone, and the up-armored M1 MOD main battle tank./nThe British contribution, among others, includes Challenger Mk.2 tanks, Stolly supply vehicles, and Warrior IFVs with dismounted Rifles squads.

Formed during World War II to fight in the Pacific, the U.S. 24th Infantry Division (Mechanized) saw further action in the Korean War. Shuffled between Europe and the United States during the Cold War, the mechanized formation was reactivated in the late ‘70s. Not earmarked as a REFORGER division, deployment to Europe for this battlegroup in case of war would have been a lengthy affair.

A mechanized division with some of the latest equipment available, the reservist National Guard will make up about a third of the 24th Infantry Division’s strength. Less experienced, fielding older small arms, vehicles, and weaponry, these American units with the Reservist traits are still capable enough when used in numbers. National Guard units include infantry squads either with Dragon or LAW anti-tank weapons in M2 Bradleys, M60 machine gun and Stinger MANPAD weapon teams, 105mm-equipped M1 Abrams, I-Tow mounted on jeeps, M109A2 self-propelled howitzers, and even A-64A Apache attack helicopters. Regular units featured are the tracked M548A2 supply, M1IP Abrams, as well as large Military Police combat squads. Protecting the skies above, one of the most advanced jet fighters flies air cover in two variants: the F-15C Eagle air superiority fighter and the F-15E Strike Eagle with laser-guided bombs.

The United States Marine Corps’ 2nd Marine Division was founded in the 1930s before famously seeing action in the Pacific Theatre of World War II, island-hopping through hard-fought victories at Guadalcanal, Tarawa, Saipan, Tinian, and Okinawa. During the Cold War, the 2nd Marine Division deployed to Lebanon in the early 1980s and to Panama for Operation Just Cause in 1989.
With the outbreak of World War III in Europe, the 2nd Marine Division was to be hurriedly ferried to Denmark in an effort to shore up the defenses of NATO’s JUTLAND command.

The 2nd Marine Division contains an arsenal of light or amphibious vehicles, underpinning the formation’s expeditionary role. This includes the LARC-60 Cargo barge, the wheeled LAV family - ranging from command, APC, and IFV to mortar carriers - as well as the AAVP-7A1 series of tracked amphibious vehicles, including a specialized mine-clearing variant, the CATFAE.
The Marines are organized into large 13-man rifle squads, backed by elite Force Recon special forces. Carrying a dual anti-air and rocket payload, the OV-10 Bronco recon plane works in tandem with the AH-1W Super Cobra, providing immediate close air support.
The USMC also fields its own organic aircraft in the form of AV-8B Harriers in various variants, plus the U.S. Navy’s poster boy of the 1980s, the formidable F-14A Tomcat air superiority fighter.

The U.S. 35th Infantry Division (Mechanized) could count on a long service record, having seen action in World War I and II. The distinctive blue cross-in-circle insignia of the formation gave rise to the “Santa Fe Division” nickname. Re-established as a mechanized infantry division in the early 1980s, with plentiful armored battalions, it acted as the missing link between the U.S. Army’s mechanized and tank divisions. The formation’s core fighting forces were further supplemented by Kansas, Missouri, Nebraska, Colorado, and Kentucky National Guard units.

The 35th Infantry Division is a true National Guard formation, with many of its N.G. units featuring the Reservist trait, from infantry to vehicles. Quite a few of the division’s weapons are old enough to have seen action during the Vietnam War. These include the small arms fielded by Rifles and Engineer squads, as well as the M60A1 main battle tank in a multitude of variants, such as the improved RISE, ERA reactive armor, and an ACAV recon version. Support includes the military police M1025 Humvee MP, the heavy M813A1 supply truck, as well as the UH-1M Gunship and the slow-moving A-37B Dragonfly available in recon and close air support variants. A special unit is the experimental XM1058 US-Roland SAM, providing air cover side-by-side with the venerable M42A1 Duster SPAAG.

The U.S. 3rd Armored Division “Spearhead” counted on a distinguished World War II career, seeing combat from Normandy all the way to VE-Day in Germany. Reactivated in the mid-1950s, one of its most famous soldiers was Elvis Presley, serving with the formation in West Germany. Part of CENTAG, the division was headquartered in and around Frankfurt. In times of conflict, as the V Corps’ heavy tank force, the 3rd Armored Division would deploy rapidly to the front, countering any Warsaw Pact incursion through the Fulda Gap.

The 3rd Armored Division relies on its tank and anti-tank units to dominate the battlefield, fielding not only the advanced M1A1 Abrams but also the M1A1(HA), one of NATO’s most heavily armored tanks. The long-range TOW-2 ATGM is present, either as part of the M901A1 ITV or as a dismounted weapon team. While infantry can only deploy as half-sized fireteams, they come in the capable Bradley IFV. Supporting units include recon M981 FISTV, heavy-duty HEMTT transports, and the M270 MRLS with Cluster warheads. Air power is another strong point: the AH-64A Apache is a potent attack helicopter, while the F-111E and F-4E Phantom II are available in various close-air support loadouts. Air superiority can be handsomely achieved with the state-of-the-art F-15C.

The U.S. 6th Infantry Division (Light) saw action in World War II before going dormant during most of the Cold War. Reactivation in 1986 saw it designated the U.S. Army’s primary Arctic Warfare division, tasked with the defense of Alaska, including key American military bases. If the far-flung Aleutian Islands were to come under attack, the division was also envisioned to take the fight across the “Ice Curtain” into the Soviet Far East. Limited in armored vehicles, the 6th Infantry Division combined various infantry, paratrooper, Navy, Air Force, and National Guard units.

The 6th Infantry Division’s core is made up of Light Rifles and Airborne Rifles squads with a variety of loadouts. Other U.S. Army equipment includes the heavy-lift CH-54B Tarhe helicopters, M119 105mm howitzers, and Vietnam War-era AH-1S Cobras. The National Guard is represented by Alaskan Scouts, the N.G. M48A5 ACAV recon tank, and the A-7D Corsair II attack aircraft. The U.S. Air Force, protecting its vital bases in the region, not only provides the recon OA-10A Thunderbolt but also USAF Security infantry squads with Peacekeeper wheeled APCs. In the same vein, the U.S. Navy fields the A-6E Intruder and EA-6B Prowler, plus USMC Security guarding naval facilities with Dragon 300 APCs, while the renowned Navy Seals provide special forces back-up.

The illustrious U.S. 82nd Airborne Division cemented its warfighting reputation with several World War II combat jumps, including the famous drops on D-Day, as well as action during Market Garden and the Battle of the Bulge. Post-war, the paratroopers formed part of the XVIII Airborne Corps’ strategic reserve and deployed to the Dominican Republic, Vietnam, and, later, Grenada in 1983. As a quick reaction force, the airborne formation would move rapidly from the continental United States to West Germany in case of hostilities.

The 82nd Airborne Division will be able to Forward Deploy most of its infantry, crew-served weapons, and vehicles, giving it a significant advantage early on in battle. Highly mobile units are the division’s hallmark, from CH-47C supply helicopters to AB M1025 TOW units, Airborne squads with AT-4s, wheeled armored reconnaissance M1047, and the M551 TTS Sheridan tank. Anti-air units include AA M998 Avengers and towed M167 Vulcan 20mm. Helicopter support is prominent, from the Zuni rocket-equipped AH-1 Heavy Hog and anti-air AH-1 ATAS to the nimble AH-6 Little Bird and modern AH-64A Apache. Air support encompasses the A-10A Thunderbolt, the potent F-15C and F-4E Phantom II in air defense roles, backed by F-16C and F-111F tactical bombers.

The U.S. 8th Infantry Division (Mechanized) saw extensive action in Europe during World War II, including taking part in the infamous Battle of Hürtgen Forest in late 1944. Reactivated in the mid-50s, the formation was headquartered in Bad Kreuznach, with subordinate brigades scattered west of Frankfurt. In the event of war, the division would have deployed either to protect Frankfurt or to join V Corps’ counterattacks against the invading Warsaw Pact.

The 8th Infantry Division counts on the excellent Mechanized Infantry in their M113 APCs, short-range Dragon ATGM-equipped soldiers, Aero Rifles with their UH-60A Black Hawk helicopter transports, and Ranger squads. Other infantry include a variety of Combat Engineers, Gunner squads, I-TOW, and TOW-2 ATGM teams. Tanks are still present, though limited in number and more expensive to deploy. These are the older M60A3 (TTS), early M1 Abrams with 105mm tank guns, and a handful of M1A1s. Artillery is potent, ranging from the M125 mortar carrier to the heavy M110A2 203mm self-propelled howitzer. The U.S. Air Force provides the modern F-16 Fighting Falcon in various loadouts for air cover. The improved F-111F makes its mark as a tactical bomber, including fielding a variant equipped with precision laser-guided bombs.

The 9th Infantry (Motorized) Division’s rich military history covered both World Wars and the Vietnam War. However, its uniqueness came to the forefront in 1981 when it became a special testbed formation for the U.S. Army. The 9th Infantry was envisioned to be light enough to deploy rapidly, but still deal with the heaviest threats. To accomplish this, it turned to an arsenal of highly advanced equipment, earning its nickname as the “Toys 'R' Us Division.” The battlegroup, with a heavy National Guard mechanized brigade, was destined to be deployed to Denmark, but with war on the horizon, would see itself redeploy into NORTHAG. 

The 9th Infantry (Motorized) Division fields two new vehicle families, one being the CUCV utility truck, the other the HMMWV or Humvee. Both are used by the division’s Light Infantry and National Guard infantry in a great variety of roles, from the M1008 CUCV Supply to the M998T Interim Squad Carrier and the recon M1025 Humvee G/VLLD. A smorgasbord of exotic units includes the M198 155mm (CLGP) with Copperhead guided ammo, the M60A1 AVLM mine-clearing vehicle, the M1008 CUCV GLH with ground-launched Hellfire missiles, the JOH-58 recon helo, the towed anti-air XM895 T-CHAP, the MQM-10 Aquila UAV, and two-person Sniper teams fielding the iconic M82 anti-materiel sniper rifle.

A Gatling gun is a multi-barrelled automatic rotary cannon capable of shooting a massive quantity of rounds extremely fast.
Using an electronic firing mechanism, a modern Gatling gun (also known as minigun) can fire so quickly it is in danger of running out of ammunition within seconds. Gatling guns are often cumbersome weapons and are relegated to be used on aircraft or stable land platforms. They can be employed as a close-in defensive system to saturate a target area by throwing a hail of fire, an anti-aircraft gun, or even an airborne anti-tank weapon able to punch through the weak top plating of many armored vehicles.
Recon units can deploy ahead of the main force. This gives them a head start. This ability is only available during a battle's initial deployment phase.

This unit excels in gathering intelligence and spotting targets. Some recon units are masters in observing the enemy undetected. Others actively scout the battlefield, using rapid mobility and light weapons to report back on enemy resistance.

Instructor units grant nearby units of the same type, either Infantry or Tank, +1 Veterancy level, while also removing any Reservist trait.

This also means their stopping power and range are less than a heavier assault rifle. Rear-echelon troops or vehicle crews frequently field submachine guns as a personal defense weapon.

An unguided or “dumb” bomb is an aerial explosive employed by aircraft or helicopters against enemy ground units. Simple and destructive, unguided bombs lack accuracy and need to be dropped over or near a target. They come in many shapes and sizes, from general HE bombs to napalm and cluster bomblets.

A tank gun is a large-caliber, high-velocity gun capable of firing various projectiles against a variety of targets.
A tank gun is the primary means of engaging other tanks or armored vehicles with direct fire. Featuring different calibers, between 90mm to 125mm, a tank gun is often emplaced in a turret, creating a flexible yet hard-hitting weapon. When assisted by advanced targeting computers and sights, a tank gun can engage almost any kind of unit, even airborne targets, regardless of the weather or time of day. A tank gun fires off a variety of different shells, at times supported by an autoloader, including armor-piercing kinetic (AP), armor-piercing, fin-stabilized, discarding sabot (APFSDS), high-explosive (HE), or high-explosive anti-tank (HEAT). Some guns can even fire specially adapted guided missiles.

Some guns can even fire specially adapted guided missiles.
Explosive Reactive Armor (ERA) is intended to counteract HEAT anti-tank munitions. It provides a boost in the survivability of the tank and its crew.
A light armored division with affordable Leopard 1 tanks, mechanized infantry, and IFVs. This Belgian battlegroup can strike early and often, but might struggle against heavier opponents.

Airborne infantry and ATGM teams, backed by large numbers of older armored vehicles, can tip the scales for this Belgian division. This rear-area mechanized battlegroup lacks helicopters and relies on a vintage arsenal, but is still a force to be reckoned with thanks to its artillery and anti-air units.

Plentiful infantry and state-of-the-art Eryx and ADATS missiles form the core of this mobile Canadian mechanized division. Backed by a massive fleet of modern F-18s, it might struggle in a head-to-head fight if its air cover is neutralized.

This well-rounded motorized rifle division can be used for a variety of offensive and defensive tasks. Capable Czechoslovakian special forces, recon, mechanized, and airmobile infantry are supported in the field by an impressive artillery arsenal.

This offensively-minded Czechoslovakian tank division is well equipped with mechanized infantry and tanks. Notable is its numerous artillery, including the short-range SVO demining vehicle, which can be used to obliterate entrenched enemy positions.

This well-balanced Czechoslovakian motorized division comprises a large contingent of infantry and border guards, supported by an array of ATGM-armed T-55AM2B tanks. This gives it a potent long-range punch, further backed by decent recon forces and artillery units.

A reserve tank division relying on older equipment, this Czechoslovakian rear-area formation is best used on defense. However, thanks to its numerical superiority and the support of a handful of modern units, the division can pose quite a challenge.
This Danish mechanized infantry division relies on older-generation armored vehicles for its punching power. Air cover is plentiful, as are its artillery and infantry forces.
A well-trained reservist division, this Danish Home Guard formation acquits itself well in a defensive fight. While the equipment might be old, American USMC air support is powerful.

Airmobile infantry with Forward Deployment and hard-hitting recon are the hallmarks of this light airborne division. Using superior mobility, the French paratrooper battlegroup keeps the enemy off-balance with ground ambushes and pinpoint air strikes.

This French stronghold division, with a diverse selection of elite special forces, is backed by a large number of reservists. Flexible and mobile, with powerful anti-air defenses and air cover, this defensive battlegroup keeps its opponents on its toes.

Rapid and mobile, this French armored division uses its wheeled tanks and strong IFVs to wreak havoc in ambushes and lightning-fast screening operations. Excellent infantry and artillery give support, but avoid going head-to-head against heavier adversaries.

Exceedingly rapid on the battlefield, this French light division leverages its fast wheeled tanks and recon for a powerful opener. Legionnaire infantry can be employed in a layered defense, but avoid being pinned down by heavier opponents.

A Franco-West German rear-area division, defensive operations are this battlegroup's strong point. Older armored vehicles are backed by numerous combat engineers, reservists, well-equipped Jäger infantry, and an array of specialized weaponry.
An armored spearhead used for heavy-hitting breakthrough operations. This Dutch division can muster a powerful combination of modern tanks, IFVs, and tank destroyers, but lacks vigorous air cover.

This second-line Dutch division features plenty of well-trained reservists, managing to execute capable combined arms operations on the battlefield. This includes American air support and the modern Leopard 2A4 tank.

This Polish mobilization division contains a small body of professional soldiers, supported by plentiful reservist units. East German naval infantry and Soviet air power boost the formation’s fighting power.

A strong recon force, together with cost-effective armored vehicles and infantry, enables this Polish tank division to perform well in all types of combat. Care should be taken against heavy or high-tech adversaries, however.

This flexible Polish mechanized division is well suited for combined-arms operations, from aggressive opening moves to massed offensives. The battlegroup is most comfortable in the early to mid-battle, thanks to its cheap tanks and mechanized infantry.

A unique half-airborne, half-naval infantry formation, the Polish battlegroup’s well-trained soldiers are specialized in fast assaults. Heavy artillery, helicopters, and air cover should deal with whatever ground threats the enemy can muster.
This East German motorized division deploys a varied array of mechanized infantry, artillery, and T-72 Tanks. Soviet armor beefs up the formation’s largely reservist core.

This East German motorized division is capable of sustaining a high tempo of combat operations. Elite airborne troops can take the ground early, with the battlegroup then switching to a defense-in-depth with its upgraded second-generation armor, helicopters, and infantry.

Closing the distance and fighting as a brawler is this East German armored battlegroup’s specialty. While the air force provides top cover, this tank division relies on superior numbers of the basic but capable T-72 to overwhelm the enemy at close range.

The favored child of the East German army, this armored division features a wide array of capable T-72 tanks and IFVs. Infantry is limited, but this tank-heavy battlegroup fights best across open terrain with its long-range missile-firing tank destroyers, artillery, and aircraft.

This division excels in high-intensity urban warfare, with some of the East Germans’ finest infantry and artillery spearheading the fight. An older arsenal means this mixed formation will have only limited options in open combat.

A rear-area defensive formation with a large number of cheap reservists and militia at its disposal. This East German division counts on excellent artillery, anti-air, logistics, and additional Soviet support, including air cover.

A mobilized East German and Polish battlegroup with numerous anti-air options. Plentiful infantry allows it to fight well when under cover, as the division can direct powerful air strikes and specialized artillery to clear out entrenched enemies.

A unique mixed air assault division with a sizable number of West German mountaineers. This formation excels in early-battle action, as well as fighting in rugged terrain, but features minimal anti-air defenses.

Strong across the board with numerous capable units, this West German mechanized infantry battlegroup includes Forward Deployable Fallschirmjägers. Counting on multinational NATO support, the battlegroup’s vulnerable to SEAD strikes, making air superiority imperative.

The pinnacle of Bundeswehr tank technology, this armored division is geared for offensive operations. Some of the most modern West German panzers, including the Leopard 2A4, can be deployed by this powerful combined-arms battlegroup.
A supersized mechanized infantry battlegroup with substantial West German Navy support. Lacking modern armor and artillery, it compensates with plentiful naval infantry and Danish air cover.

A rear-area defensive division, with West German reservists joined by French airmobile and American special forces. Powerful anti-air units and artillery, plus a unique mix of aircraft, compensate for the battlegroup’s older equipment, tanks, and ATGM troops.

An unstoppable juggernaut late in the battle, this armored spearhead is built for high-intensity tank warfare. Its expensive state-of-the-art Soviet tanks, air, and special forces take time to build up in sufficient numbers.

A Soviet mobilization division based in the Crimea filled with mothballed equipment and reservists. An eclectic mix of weaponry, including Soviet Navy assets, can give this defensive battlegroup’s untrained mass of infantry a surprising punch on the battlefield.
A Soviet reservist mobilization division with an eclectic arsenal of older tanks, artillery, and even World War II-era assault guns. Best used in close-range defensive fights,

Armored superiority for this Soviet tank division comes in the form of massed T-64s. A unique but unbalanced organization results in deficiencies in logistics and infantry, which are offset by artillery and heavily armored recon troops.

With the latest Soviet Army equipment at its disposal, this modern combined-arms battlegroup merges plentiful mechanized IFVs and infantry with potent artillery. Its high-end units are powerful, but limited in number.

This honorific Moscow-based formation is a highly motivated infantry division with access to some of the most advanced units of the Soviet Army. The straightforward combined arms approach sees its well-trained Gvardeitsy squads team up with state-of-the-art T-80U tanks.

An arsenal of T-72s, along with numerous infantry, allows this Soviet tank division to hold any territory it gains comfortably. Air and helicopter support might be meagre, but artillery more than compensates.

This elite Soviet naval infantry division excels at spearheading amphibious assaults on contested shores. Strong “Black Death” infantry, capable tanks, and potent air support make up the division’s offensive firepower on the battlefield.

This well-trained Soviet air assault division excels in fast-moving operations and aggressive opening attacks. It contains a high ratio of Forward Deployable mechanized vehicles, light but heavily armed, supported by special forces and advanced Ka-50 attack helicopters.

An archetypal Soviet motorized rifle division, with a balanced arsenal across its armored, helicopter, and mechanized infantry forces. This battlegroup performs equally well in offensive and defensive operations.

A versatile half-mechanized Soviet air assault division with numerous veteran soldiers, Spetzaz special forces, and a host of unorthodox field-modified vehicles. With unrivaled battlefield mobility, this battlegroup's arsenal is equally colorful as it is powerful.

A Soviet combined-arms battlegroup with key East German support. An array of cheap bombers and infantry, with a few airmobile troops, allows it to fight well in urban or rugged terrain. Air defense, with its long-range AA units and interceptors, is another strong point.

With an emphasis on mechanization, this Soviet airborne battlegroup relies on its state-of-the-art armored vehicles and air cover for its battlefield firepower. Light but hard-hitting, the battlegroup lacks in air assault capabilities and helicopter gunships.

A top-notch armored division capable of brute-forcing its way through stiff opposition. From main battle tanks to heavy bombers, this Soviet battlegroup takes time to build up its strength on the battlefield.

A lavishly equipped Soviet mechanized infantry division deploying earlier variants of the T-64s in great numbers. Further backed by powerful recon and combat engineers, the battlegroup lacks in supporting arms, critically so in helicopter and air support.

A renowned Soviet Army formation in which regular and reserve forces work in close cooperation. Cheap T-72s and infantry shield the division’s arsenal of powerful anti-tank units, but with few ways to mask an attack, care should be taken on the battlefield.

This Spanish light cavalry division relies on its fast recon forces to aggressively seize territory early in a battle. Hold gains with cheap armor and wheeled tank destroyers, backed by capable supporting arms and air cover.

This light Spanish motorized division is centered around the BMR APC and fast infantry units. The lack of forward deployment options is compensated by a plethora of light armor and recon, backed by a well-balanced selection of artillery.

A heavy brawler, this British armored division deals damage with its advanced long-range ATGM carriers, while its more than capable tanks advance under fire. Air cover is likewise formidable, from air defense to closer air support.

This British division is strong in the early battle due to its airmobile troops and powerful SAS special forces. Battlefield mobility is excellent, as is its infantry, which should be used to create a long-lasting defense in depth.

This British armored formation has a well-balanced arsenal of competent infantry, armor, and air support. It can outlast the enemy in any scrappy brawl, as long as the division’s mix of older equipment is put to good and careful use.

This multinational infantry division under British command is honed to fight on urban battlefields. Strong in early recon pushes, defense is the battlegroup's strength, with stealthy strikes and massive raids by its potent bomber force keeping the enemy at bay.

The Queen’s Guard is one of the many unusual units in this unique composite but highly motivated London-based defensive garrison, which also includes counter-terror SAS squads and ceremonial artillery guns.

The multinational mix of various NATO airmobile units, each with a well-balanced roster of paratroopers, infantry, and vehicles. This light but flexible airborne division is equally comfortable in close-combat operations as in long-range defense.

An excellent roster of airmobile infantry and special forces form the beating heart of this hard-and-fast American airborne battlegroup. Favoring early aggressive pushes, a powerful flying arsenal of helicopters, gunships, and aircraft backs up the boots on the ground.

With excellent recon, tank, and air units, this mechanized battlegroup is best used offensively. Aggressive tactics early on can derail enemy plans, all the while the division builds up to unleash scores of M1A1 Abrams for a mighty late-battle armored push.

The distinguished American division fields a wide array of capable tanks, further bolstered by British armor. With few infantry, this Anglo-American battlegroup deploys several unique Abrams and Bradley variants, dominating the open range.

Bolstered by a core of regulars, this American mechanized infantry division can also deploy National Guard units, giving commanders access to numerous cheap but strong forces. Air power is especially formidable, with the F-15E Strike Eagle more than capable of picking off high-value targets.

An uniquely distinct American battlegroup, the iconic USMC expeditionary task force fields a potent mix of marines, air, recon, and helicopter forces. Logistics and heavier arms, such as artillery and tanks, are on the light side, however.

A well-rounded National Guard battlegroup, in which numerous second-generation M60A1 main battle tanks can be deployed en masse. Excellent air defense and ground strike aircraft act as potent force multipliers.

The tip of the spear, this offensively geared American division contains powerful high-end armor, IFVs, and aircraft. Slow to open, expensive to deploy, and with small infantry squads, the battlegroup's full potential typically unlocks late into a battle.

A mix of airborne and reserve infantry fills up the ranks of this defensive-minded Arctic Warfare battlegroup. Lacking heavy armor, the American multi-service division’s very powerful air support is the ticket to victory.

First to fight, this American airborne division prides itself on opening strong with Forward Deployed paratroopers and excellent recon vehicles. Supported by top-end aircraft and helicopter forces, this light battlegroup should avoid being cornered by combined-arms opponents in unfavorable terrain.

A strong combined-arms American battlegroup, with an edge in infantry and Ranger squads, supported by potent artillery and air units. While the division lacks speed, its firepower is more than capable of bleeding the enemy dry over time.

This high-tech American motorized division dominates the fight with hit-and-run attacks and ambushes. Mobile wheeled ATGM destroyers allow the versatile but light battlegroup to fend off enemy armor, with its National Guard contingent providing additional staying power.
An infantry assault squad is specialized in close-range combat in urban or built-up terrain.

An incendiary rocket launcher is a specialized man-portable weapon capable of firing incendiary or thermobaric warheads. The warhead is often confused for napalm, but the incendiary rocket launcher in many ways better resembles a stand-off flamethrower. 

Incendiary rocket launchers are effective against enemy infantry and buildings.
Assault squads are infantry specialized in short-range combat, particularly in urban terrain.
Security units increase their Optics and spotting abilities to Good when not moving. They remain classified as Infantry.

Armored vehicle designed to carry infantry into battle and provide direct-fire support. The Infantry Fighting Vehicle (IFV) is typically armored and armed with potent weapons, including ATGMs. This allows them to be effective against an array of ground targets, from enemy infantry to tanks.

This unit is composed of law enforcement, civilians, or paramilitary personnel, raised to active duty to support a nation’s regular military. While trained, they typically lack front-line combat experience or instruction in heavy weaponry and equipment.

This unit is composed of soldiers who are highly motivated, well-drilled, or politically indoctrinated. Going into battle with plenty of enthusiasm, these eager troops will endure even the hardest battlefield conditions in stride.

A small, hand-held explosive that can be thrown by an individual soldier.
Grenades can be encountered in many shapes and sizes, including fragmentation anti-personal, smoke grenades, gas, or even anti-tank grenades. As extremely close-range weapons, they are used in various combat situations, including clearing houses or bunkers, thrown into vehicles, or as boobytraps. Due to proximity and sometimes large blast radius, grenades are often equally dangerous to the user as to the enemy.

A submachine gun is a quick-firing, short-range firearm.
Submachine guns (SMGs) fire smaller cartridges, most often used in handguns, which allows for a more compact and easier to wield automatic weapon. This also means their stopping power and range are less than a heavier assault rifle. Rear-echelon troops or vehicle crews frequently field submachine guns as a personal defense weapon.

The standard weapon for a large number of frontline soldiers, the battle rifle is effective against enemy troops at intermediate ranges.
Heavy and powerful, battle rifles are very accurate and deadly when the shooter is immobile, but quite less than an assault rifle on the move, especially since it uses smaller magazines. Most assault rifles can be modified with accessories such as scopes, foregrips, night vision devices, or single-shot grenade launchers.

This unit is an Unmanned Aerial Vehicle, a drone piloted from a the ground by an operator and used for reconnaissance. Small, slow & silent, it is hard to spot by the human eye and intended to be discarded as a bird by radars.
This unit features the oft-detested military police. As law enforcement, they ensure order behind the lines and instill harsh discipline within an army’s ranks.

An air-to-ground missile (AGM) is designed to be launched from aircraft against ground targets. Depending on the combat role, various propulsion, warheads, and guidance modes are available. Most AGMs are fire-and-forget, while some require active or semi-active guidance onto a target.

Air-to-ground missiles are potent stand-off weapons. They are useful in surgical strikes against spotted high-value targets such as main battle tanks, air defense systems, artillery, and command units. Older-generation AGMs might lack accuracy.
Air-dropped explosive weapon that ejects small unguided cluster bombs.

A submachine gun (SMG) is a quick-firing, short-range firearm. This type of weapon fires smaller caliber rounds, which allows for a more compact automatic weapon. SMGs are frequently fielded by assault infantry or rear-echelon troops and vehicle crews as a personal defense weapon.

A submachine gun's range, accuracy, and damage are less than that of an assault rifle. The rate of fire is higher, making them better suited for close or urban combat.

An air-to-air missile (AAM) is one of the primary weapons aircraft use to destroy airborne targets. Optimized for a specific range envelope, these sophisticated weapons feature different propulsion methods, warheads, and guidance modes, such as radar or heat-seeking.

Some AAMs are designed for long-distance combat with a preference for speed and range. Short-range missiles emphasize maneuverability and are most often used during dogfights.
An Unmanned Aerial Vehicle (UAV) is a remotely piloted drone. UAVs fly reconnaissance missions, providing battlefield surveillance without putting a human pilot at risk.

This unit is composed of soldiers trained to fight with an Infantry Fighting Vehicle (IFV). Following an army's mechanized infantry doctrine, the troops work closely with an IFV once dismounted. This way soldiers take full advantage of the vehicle's armor, weapons, and sensors.

Mortars are indirect-fire crew-served infantry weapons capable of lobbing shells in high trajectories across medium distances.
Mortars come in various calibers, from 50mm to 120mm to the occasional massive 240mm. Caliber size determines their range, how easily they can be transported, rate of fire, and destructive power. Some larger units are vehicle-mounted on dedicated carriers, allowing quick displacement after shooting. Capable of firing off different types of rounds, from high-explosive to smoke or illumination, mortars provide indispensable organic fire support on the battlefield.

An Laser Guided Bomb (LGB) is an explosive employed by aircraft against enemy ground units.
Simple and destructive, guided bombs are also known as GBU(Guided Bomb Unit). A disadvantage is that bombs dropped as a payload need to have the user fly over a target, but are rather accurate. Guided bombs can come in many shapes and sizes.

Unguided air-to-ground rockets are fired from aircraft and helicopters at ground targets.
A common weapon, rockets normally lack an active guidance system, separating them from missiles. A simple and easy-to-use weapon - though not very accurate - rockets are convenient in a short-range or area saturation role. Carrying various types of warheads, rockets are frequently fired from rocket pods in devastating salvoes.
Units equipped with Smoke Launchers can create a single-use smoke screen by pressing B or SMOKE in the order panel.

An autocannon can rapidly fire medium-sized caliber rounds, including HE and armor piercing. This weapon is devestating against infantry and lightly armored and soft-skinned vehicles. Different types of autocannons can be found as the primary armament on a host of vehicles, from armored personnel carriers to helicopter gunships.

Autocannons are effective against an array of targets.
Military Police units grant a suppression regeneration bonus to nearby allies and remove any Reservist traits from them.
A half-sized infantry squad. They specialize in close-range combat in urban terrain.

This unit is equipped with an Active Protection System, designed to intercept incoming guided missiles with hard-kill defensive charges. The device’s narrow engagement envelope and number of charges limits the system's effectiveness, and its reaction time prevents it from intercepting supersonic missiles.

Active Protection System protects its host unit only against guided missiles within a short interception range in a narrow 180° forward arc. The defensive charges can damage nearby friendly infantry.
This light vehicle or towed gun is designed to be airlifted by large helicopters as part of tactical air assault operations.

A surface-to-air missile (SAM) is launched from a ground platform at airborne targets. Like other missile families, SAMs are designed around an effective engagement envelope, using different types of warheads, propulsion methods, and guidance systems to track, intercept, and destroy airplanes. Surface-to-air missiles are fired from a mobile platform typically housing radar and tracking equipment.

SAMs are designed to be effective at various targets and ranges. Some use active radar, while others home in automatically using infrared.

Aircraft specialized in electronic warfare. This unit is equipped with countermeasures and powerful devices to detect or jam enemy radar and signals. They are employed near or over enemy territory, locating and disrupting radar-equipped units.

This unit is armed with precision-guided munitions, such as Laser-Guided Bombs (LGBs) or Cannon-Launched Guided Projectiles (CLGPs). Highly accurate, these ranged weapons can be guided onto a target with a laser designator.
Mortars are crew-served indirect-fire weapons. While capable of engaging targets rapidly, mortars do not have a great range and lack accuracy.
Counter-Battery Radar units feature an Area of Effect, which reveals an enemy artillery unit the moment they fire, regardless of the terrain. The location is lost once the enemy unit ceases firing.

Anti-Air (AA) guns are weapons designed to take out fast-moving airborne targets.
These types of guns are frequently emplaced in quick traversing turrets with a high rate of fire and elevation. In this way, with more advanced systems using targeting computers and radar, they can track and shoot at aircraft and helicopters at a moment’s notice. AA guns are often found in dual or even quadruple mounts. In addition, these guns are frequently used for great effect in a direct-fire role against lightly armored ground targets.

An Anti-Tank Rocket Launcher is a shoulder-fired weapon designed to take out armored or reinforced land targets.
These launchers fire an unguided rocket-propelled anti-tank projectile, giving the regular combat soldier an efficient, portable weapon to neutralize enemy tanks or vehicles. They are short-range weapons, best used in ambushes or from cover such as buildings or forests.
Recon units have excellent Optics and Stealth. This allows them to scout the battlefield and spot enemy targets, while trying to remain undetected.
IFV Infantry units take less Suppression in combat when near an Infantry Fighting Vehicle.
This specialized leader unit is equipped with fire-control systems, sensors, communication devices, and other equipment to improve the indirect fire of subordinate artillery guns.
The tank is a heavily armored vehicle, effective against any type of ground target.

A tank gun is a large-caliber, high-velocity gun capable of firing projectiles against ground targets. A tank gun fires off a variety of different shells, including armor-piercing kinetic (AP), armor-piercing, fin-stabilized, discarding sabot (APFSDS), high-explosive (HE), or high-explosive anti-tank (HEAT). Some guns can even fire specially adapted guided missiles. A tank gun's caliber determines range and firepower. 

The tank gun is the primary means of engaging infantry, other tanks, or armored vehicles with direct fire.

The assault rifle is the standard combat firearm for the vast majority of soldiers. Effective across short- to medium-range, a great variety of assault rifles have developed, from compact variants to more accurate semi-automatic or burst-fire and automatic rifles. Different calibers affect mobility, range, and firepower. 

Assault rifles are effective against enemy infantry and certain lightly armored targets.

The anti-tank rocket launcher is a shoulder-fired weapon designed to take out armored vehicles. These launchers fire unguided rocket-propelled projectiles, which can feature a variety of warheads, including HE and HEAT. This is an effective stand-off weapon, great at neutralizing tanks or other ground targets.

Due to its short range, anti-tank rocket launchers are best used in ambushes or from cover. More advanced models have better armor penetration and destructive power, including tandem-warheads.
Units designed specifically to engage and destroy enemy tanks and armored vehicles.
This unit is trained to be inserted onto the battlefield through the air. Highly mobile but lightly equipped, airborne troops can rapidly deploy ahead of the regular army.
Resolute units take less Suppression in combat.

Mortars are crew-served indirect-fire weapons capable of lobbing shells in high trajectories across short- to medium distances. Simple breach-loaded weapons mortars come in various calibers which determine range, mobility, and destructive power. Some larger units are vehicle mounted.

Mortars can quickly fire off different types of shells, from HE to smoke. They provide vital close-fire support on the battlefield.
A half-sized infantry squad with a reduced complement of soldiers. This smaller infantry unit is easier to transport but has less firepower and strength.
This unit features hardened soldiers specifically trained and equipped for close-quarter battles, assault operations, and hand-to-hand combat.

A fast-flying missile launched from an aircraft or helicopter for the purpose of destroying airborne targets.
Air-to-air missiles can be broadly divided into two categories: those designed to engage hostile aircraft at very short range, also known as within visual range missiles; and those that fly far and neutralize targets beyond visual range. Short-range missiles frequently feature rapid rocket motors and heat-seeking guidance systems. Long-range missiles often use slower jet engines and radar guidance to engage hostile aircraft across considerable distances.

A medium machine gun is a crew-served infantry weapon capable of automatic fire at intermediate ranges.\This type of belt-fed machine gun is light enough to be transported by individual soldiers, but most often needs a small crew to be operated effectively. Medium machine guns fire, almost in all cases, 5,56mm (NATO) or 7.62mm (Warsaw Pact) rounds, which can also be used in other small arms. Medium machine guns are frequently featured as primary weapons on soft-skinned and lightly armed vehicles or as coaxial armament in heavier units.
